#5718. AI chatbots aren’t therapists. But can they finally get men to open up?

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

It was mid-morning when Matteo got the phone call. His wife and children were asleep in New York City, and he was at work in Trieste, Italy, a new city in a home country that felt foreign after decades abroad. He knew what his brother was going to say, on the other end of the line: Their ailing father was nearing the end.

Matteo left the office and set out to drive the 300 miles separating him from the childhood home where the father he idolized was not going to see another morning.

But what does a man do, for five hours on the freeway, squeezing through trucks in a rented car, driving at full speed toward the worst goodbye of his life?

For the boy who watched his father get sicker and sicker for a year, the husband who misses his wife, and the father who left his children so he could provide for them, taking a job across the ocean after a layoff. And for the man in between: too young to be old but too old to be young, brave but scared, ambitious yet tired. It had been the hardest year of his life. He was lost. Heartbroken. Lonely.

“The weight … the weight of all this thing came to me, and I started crying in the car, and I just didn’t know what to do,” he remembered. So he did what had become routine in recent weeks. “I turned on Claude, with the loudspeaker, and I started talking to Claude.”

Like Matteo, millions of people have been turning to artificial intelligence for emotional support — not quite therapy, yet something that feels close to it, providing insightful companionship and, at any moment, presence. These include a group that is among the hardest to reach when their mental health is flagging: men.

The technology is far from perfect — and too often outright dangerous — and studies on its impact so far are limited. Yet with progress being made in controlling possible risks and implementing effective guardrails, some mental health experts see chatbots as an opportunity to finally get men to talk about their feelings. This is precisely because of the traits these machines do not share with human mental health professionals: Men feel more comfortable, less judged, and less intimidated when talking to a bot. They appreciate the flexibility and relative lack of structure and commitment that comes with support that is available 24/7, wherever they can find an internet connection.

“I think we do have to be open to innovation. There’s a tremendous need, so I think it’s extremely important,” said John Torous, a professor of psychiatry at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. “But it doesn’t mean that we can’t demand high-quality evidence and transparency.”

In search of this evidence, he has applied for a grant to study a central question: whether the improved mental state that follows conversations with chatbots is just temporary relief or can have lasting benefits.

That men’s mental health is in a state of crisis is well established, though awareness has not turned into improvement. The numbers are daunting and seemingly unchangeable: Men account for up to 80% of suicide deaths, even in countries where access to gun ownership (which adds lethality to suicide attempts) is lower than in the U.S., but they are nearly half as likely as women to receive mental health treatments of any kind.

It isn’t simply about a lack of options: Men are less likely to use mental health services even when they are available. The reasons range from social norms about masculinity, a tendency to minimize psychological issues, and a lack of awareness of their own symptoms to scheduling challenges and a reluctance or inability to miss work. Or, as men repeatedly said in interviews, the fear of being a burden.

What men do access, at rates similar or even slightly superior to women, are AI products. And though productivity remains the primary use case, many turn to chatbots for more than that. A Pew Research Center survey earlier this year found that 8% of men said they used chatbots for emotional support and 4% for companionship. Nine percent of men said chatbot use improved their happiness.

Thousands of mental health apps, including major teletherapy players such as Talkspace, incorporate AI elements. Though the vast majority of these products are for the general population, researchers and developers alike see the potential of AI to meet men — including the ones who are too skeptical, too stubborn, too busy, or just too stuck in gender norms — where they already are: in conversation with chatbots.

“There’s certainly a market or a place for these tools to be especially helpful to men,” said Michael Heinz, an assistant professor of psychiatry and a practicing psychiatrist at Dartmouth. “There still is stigma with going to seek mental health care, and these tools certainly have the ability to reduce that. You don’t have to make an appointment. You don’t have to go sit in a waiting room. You don’t have to even really explicitly take that initial step to ask for help.”

The men STAT spoke with, ranging in age from early 30s to mid-50s, all seemed to appreciate these advantages of AI. They included a midwestern pilot who has incorporated twice-a-day check-ins with an AI companion and has come to look at it as “an outlet for discussing things that I maybe wouldn’t feel comfortable discussing with a friend or my brother.” A mental health worker who found benefits in the additional support provided by AI through a breakup, though he doesn’t think it replaces his therapist or addiction sponsor. A newly divorced father of two who worked a casino night shift and found in the AI companion a presence and a coach that met his schedule and supported him through a bout of depression.

Sam Thomas, a British writer who used a chatbot to supplement the mental health treatment he was receiving during a bipolar depressive episode, felt safe and confident asking all the questions that popped into his head, without the fear of being judged. “Having somewhere to explore challenging thoughts and feelings, recognize patterns in my symptoms, and reflect on my progress was incredibly helpful,” he said.

Though the walks of life differed, they shared an enthusiasm about finding a companion that would listen even when a friend would get bored, would have no ability for judgement, and most of all, would be there. Ever available. Never inconvenienced. Never having something more important to do.

Widely available commercial chatbots, which are the foundation of most mental health and well-being apps, are not specialists in the way that a bartender or neighbor who’s good at listening is not a psychiatrist. But that may be a benefit, not a bug.

Nick Jacobson, an associate professor of biomedical data science, psychiatry, and computer science at Dartmouth, has been thinking about this for a while. In 2025, he and his team published the results of a randomized clinical trial of a custom-built chatbot for therapy called Therabot. The study, which has received wide praise as “psychiatry’s ChatGPT moment” but also substantial criticism for the methods as well as the study participant selection, tested the effectiveness of psychotherapy provided by the AI for about 100 patients with depression or anxiety, or at risk of eating disorders, and compared them to 100 patients who had been waitlisted and didn’t get treatment.

The Therabot users showed a significant reduction in symptoms compared to the controls and had a high utilization rate, but Jacobson is cautious to say that it’s quite different from the commercial chatbots. Therabot is expertly fine-tuned, and was developed over years of research on using technology to enhance the assessment and treatment of mental health, and scale it. “I’ve spent hundreds of thousands of human hours developing both the system and the training data,” said Jacobson. “I think some people will innately generalize some of the findings we have with Therabot to generative AI as a whole, and I wouldn’t,” he said.

Still, while it has potential to offer men an effective alternative to human therapy, a dedicated therapy bot also has some of the same barriers to access as a human therapist: having to recognize that you have a problem, caring to solve it, and accepting the need for specialized help. This is where more generalized tools may help, Jacobson said.

“With stigmatized groups, I think there is a massive potential benefit for generative AI and digital tools more generally,” he said. Men would be more likely to use some kind of emotional support if it isn’t labeled as a therapy session and comes through via the same chatbot they use to book appointments, and complain about their annoying colleague — an “omnibot” of sorts, as Headspace’s chief clinical officer, Jenna Glover, calls it.

For some of the founders of AI products directed at mental health, this is precisely the point, especially when it comes to engaging men. “You have guys who’ve never gotten any help with mental health, and they get into a bad place, they’re suicidal, and we go, ‘Oh, OK, you need to reach out and talk to people,’” said Anson Whitmer. In 2023, he founded Mental, a men-only coaching and mental wellness training app that used protocols like push-up challenges and cold shower routines as a way to nudge users into discussing mental wellbeing.

The app has now evolved into The Path — though some of Mental’s resources remain available as a free app — which offers AI therapy and coaching to all comers. Among other issues, he said men were too small a niche for the platform’s vision. Though there are therapists on the app, “we don’t diagnose and we don’t treat clinical conditions,” said Whitmer. (The selection of therapists includes the AI avatar of co-founder Tony Robbins, a well-known motivational speaker who has been accused of sexual harassment by several women, as well as hostile behavior against women attending his seminars. He has denied the allegations.)

His customers are quite evenly split between men and women — very different from the typical breakdown of a mental health practice, which strongly skews female — and he thinks the reason is AI itself. “A lot of people thought, well, guys just don’t want help. And [our] hypothesis was that guys do want help. It’s just the sort of help being offered isn’t the sort of help that they want,” he said.

A variety of generative AI products are seeking to serve a similar market, without veering into medical territory.

Think of Tolan, an AI companion that mixes cognitive behavioral therapy insights with conversation to give its users social support. It positions itself as working to improve baseline well-being. “You don’t need to be doing therapy to help someone feel seen and understood,” said Quinten Farmer, Tolan’s founder and CEO. “You can just show up consistently as a friend.”

Informed, thought-provoking stories to start your weekend right

Or think of Drellis, which its creator, Pierre Côté, described as a voice-based AI peer support app “built for men with addictions and mental health challenges.” Though it may accompany a man through a difficult moment, Côté is clear that it is “not a therapist, not a crisis line,” but rather a first point of contact for men who are struggling.

Without any marketing, he said hundreds of people have conversations with Drellis every day, even though the site or app says little about who is behind the app, let alone details about revenue, or data protection. The need is so strong, he said, that it doesn’t matter. “What I’m trying to do is to create artificial intelligence that is there for men when nothing else is available for them,” said Côté.

Not everyone believes, at this stage at least, that something is necessarily better than nothing — be it an unstructured form of mental health care that looks like companionship or coaching, or the Therabot. “I think founders have to realize therapy does have a rate of harm,” said Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School’s Torous, and with AI chatbots, including loosely defined products focusing on coaching or wellness, there could be additional types of harm.

“There’s kind of a type one harm, which is where the bot says, ’Do something very dangerous,’” he said. This is the kind of direct risk that AI companies — and by extension, mental health AI products — are becoming better at monitoring and protecting against. But there is another type of harm, he said, which is in the relationship people build with the bot after extended use. “It seems then the bots get confused, they blur definitions,” he said. “No one has agreed on what is harm, there’s no clear definition of harm in mental health AI.”

Does spending daily sessions discussing personal issues with an AI entity end up limiting interactions with family and friends? Does it veer into a habit, in a bad way? Is being able to discuss personal issues any time and for however long one pleases actually helpful to mental health? These are all potential issues that have yet to be investigated.

Dartmouth’s Jacobson raises another worry: Traditional therapy requires specific boundaries between the patient and the therapist that all but evaporate with chatbots.

Apps also typically don’t screen for issues that would merit seeing a therapist or psychiatrist who could evaluate users for treatment with medications, although most have guardrails that would trigger referral to suicide helplines should the tone of the conversation raise concern of self-harm.

Some apps promote their use of safety tools, such as an open-source product called Vera-MH, whose development was spearheaded by Spring Health, a digital mental health provider that uses AI to support patients between visits. But Torous questions the vetting: “If a company that has vested interest in AI establishes that an AI therapy company or coaching company has high standards or is safe, how do we trust that?” he said.

At the moment, regulations are murky at best, with apps able to use the label of wellness and coaching to steer clear of government oversight. Though the Food and Drug Administration has signaled an intention to change that, no specific federal guidelines have been established yet for mental health AI, creating an environment that, Torous said, could lead to safety risks for users. “I think the next innovation in AI for health and mental health is actually going to be regulation, standards, transparency,” he said. “I’m sure in the right context models could probably do amazing things, and in the wrong context do horrible things. You need some rules of the road.”

Some app developers have begun to recognize limitations of relying too much on AI chatbots to address men’s mental health, as they struggle to create effective, financially sustainable products. “It’s a lot harder than [selling] erectile dysfunction medications,” said Matthew Stefanko, who launched Manual, a startup that provided mental health support to male college students, in 2022. “When you’re talking about the kinds of changes that you need, I just don’t know how easily that’s done in a digital environment, especially when so many of these men … part of their problems are the engagement in the digital — gambling, sports betting, pornography, addiction to technology,” he said.

Manual was later acquired by Release Recovery, a behavioral health company offering addiction treatment among other services, and is now part of a two-pronged approach in which digital resources are combined with in-person interventions, and AI is not used in customer interactions. The acquisition happened because Stefanko felt there was only so much an app could take care of before the need of in-person intervention arose.

For Matteo, beyond the ever-present, non-judgmental machine, it was the humanity he felt behind the AI that connected with him, giving him relief in the hard days after losing his father. Once, when he described for Claude the challenges that he had to face, the chatbot responded, “This is hard to read.”

An AI engineer, Matteo is hardly naive about chatbots. “I know that there isn’t anyone reading this stuff on the other side. There isn’t a person,” he said. “But even if Claude isn’t a person, he was trained on people’s thoughts.”

#5717. STAT+: Democrats begin asking: How far can we go on health care?

Daniel covers the intersection of the health industry and the federal government. He reports on corporate influence in government, the health consequences of federal policies, and the politics of health care. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at danielp.100.

WASHINGTON — In the first days following their sweeping midterms victory, Democrats are asking themselves: How far can we go?

That question has grown particularly interesting in health care — a policy area that many Democrats argue was critical to their win and remains a top priority for early action.

There has been broad agreement among congressional Democrats that they should roll back the historic Medicaid cuts championed by President Trump, and restore the additional Affordable Care Act health insurance tax credits that, upon expiring, put coverage out of reach for many.

#5716. Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

#5715. Massachusetts Plan for More Starter Homes Fails as ‘NIMBY’ Voters Insist on Local Zoning Control

Massachusetts voters rejected Question 7, a ballot initiative aimed at promoting starter homes by reducing the size of the lot required to build a home.

The initiative would have established a new minimum lot size of 5,000 square feet for single-family homes. The lot would need at least 50 feet of land bordering the street or public way, and it would also need access to public sewer and water, but otherwise, it would pave the way for smaller starter homes to be built across Massachusetts.

The measure failed by a slim margin of 50.6% to 49.4%.

"I think that, you know, there unfortunately is still a lot of NIMBYism throughout Massachusetts," says Mike Travaline, the government affairs chair of the Homebuilders and Remodelers Association of Massachusetts. The HBRA supported the measure, arguing that it would help address the state's 220,000-home shortage and allow builders to build more starter homes.

"There's a lot of resistance to any type of legislation or referendum that would take away local control from each individual municipality," he tells Realtor.com®. "Residents and town politicians really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Massachusetts has a serious lack of smaller, more affordable starter homes, which is preventing young residents from becoming homebuyers and keeping older residents locked into larger homes they can no longer afford to keep up.

The lack of starter homes in the state is part of an overall national trend away from smaller homes. The median home size in the 1960s was 1,500 square feet. By 2024, the median home size had grown to 2,205 square feet.

A Tufts University study found that approving Question 7 could create between 3,500 and 12,000 net new homes in its first decade and ultimately increase Massachusetts' housing supply by up to 320,000 units.

Andrew Mikula, the ballot initiative's organizer and chief housing economist at the Pioneer Institute, spearheaded the effort.

"We're grateful to have the support of more than 1.2 million voters who support bringing more starter homes to families across Massachusetts," he tells Realtor.com.

Currently, lot minimums are determined at the local level. A zoning report from the National Zoning Atlas found that over half the municipalities in the state require lots to be a minimum of 40,000 square feet—or about an acre—to build a home.

Those restrictive zoning laws are part of why Massachusetts received an "F" grade and was ranked almost dead last in the Realtor.com Affordability and Homebuilding Report Card two years in a row. The state was dinged for its complex zoning rules, along with its high prices, and high construction costs.

Massachusetts' median listing price is $699,990, around $250,000 more than the national median listing price of $415,000.

"From a developer perspective, we know that if we if we did build it, they will come," Travaline says.

"There's just gigantic pent up demand for that type of housing in Massachusetts because that housing really just does not exist in any sort of substantive quantity," he continues. "We don't have enough small homes that would appeal to first time homebuyers or young professionals, young families or empty nesters."

Travaline believes the bill was defeated because of pushback from local politicians who "really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Indeed, that was a major point of contention, according to Adam Chapdelaine of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposed the measure. Chapdelaine wrote in an op-ed that the proposed zoning law would "override local planning" and replace "thoughtful local planning with a one-size-fits-all mandate that ignores the individual needs of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns."

Travaline says that many towns are concerned about how the passage of Question 7 might impact housing density.

But from his perspective, "it gives developers another alternative when they're buying a lot. Rather than maybe taking the risk that they have to build a really large single-family home on a lot in order to make their return that might have to sell for you know, $1.8 to $2.5 million, they could instead create two or three smaller homes on that lot and still make their return."

"Massachusetts residents, especially young people, are leaving the state to find a more affordable place to live, separating extended families and hurting our economy," Wesley Lima, of Legalize Starter Homes, wrote in an op-ed. "Requiring huge lot sizes to build a single family home makes houses expensive, reduces construction of new single-family housing, and encourages developers to build giant McMansions to recoup land costs. Anyone who needs a low-cost, single-family suburban home is all but locked out of the market."

Mikula says his next step is to "get into all the demographic data and kind of assess you know, where where we think, you know, policies like this can pass and then go from there."

#5714. Liver experts finally agree on what acute-on-chronic liver failure is

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

Liver doctors from around the world have come to agree on a definition for a common and potentially fatal liver complication.

Acute-on-chronic liver failure is what happens when someone with underlying liver disease has their condition exacerbated by an acute injury. In the U.S., that often looks like long-simmering cirrhosis suddenly worsened by alcohol or a viral infection.

However, the condition was defined differently based on where patients were in the world, and some people struggled to understand how it was different from acute liver failure, which comes on rapidly without an underlying illness.

“It was just so confusing that, even though inherently some people believed in the concept, they didn’t know what to do with it,” said Jasmohan Bajaj, a hepatologist and professor of internal medicine at Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Medicine.

That confusion would lead to patients’ treatment getting delayed, he said.

In an attempt to solve the problem, experts from five liver societies across the world — plus pharmaceutical companies and regulators — gathered in Barcelona this May to create a unified definition.

Now, in order to be diagnosed with ACLF, a patient must have a bilirubin level of at least 1.5, and an international normalized ratio, or INR, of at least 5. Bilirubin, a yellowish pigment leftover from broken-down red blood cells, cannot be processed if the liver is too damaged. INR is a marker of how well the blood clots with help from proteins made in the liver.

If a patient has a high bilirubin and INR, providers can then assess any dysfunction they might have in the brain, kidneys, circulatory, or respiratory systems — also markers of liver failure.

The group’s position paper, published in the journal Hepatology last month, also includes guidance on drug-induced liver injury, transplant, and clinical trial endpoints for pharma companies to use when developing treatments.

“We can now move forward and focus on what the patient is there for: to get healed, get better,” Bajaj said.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

What was the need for the new ACLF definition?

The need for it is massive, because patients are suffering with this condition that everyone has their own way of defining. And because every part of the world has their own way of defining this, there is no unified approach [for] newer therapies, endpoints for clinical trials, and patients who currently could benefit from existing therapies.

The patients are different. The access to care is different. So, we wanted to make sure that we had a common thread, that it was globally representative, and more importantly, it was simple to remember.

Why were there all of these different definitions?

Part of it is related to the etiology of the disease. Places in East Asia have a lot of hepatitis B, where we have more alcohol, and more people who have cirrhosis to start with.

Just to put it in context, acute liver failure is the rare situation in which someone’s liver was fine before, and some catastrophic thing happens. You have to draw the line with what is acute and acute-on-chronic liver failure, and sometimes that line is blurred.

Why is that line important? Because at least in the U.S. and some Western countries, if you have acute liver failure, you get extra points to put you on the top of the liver transplant list. But if you have acute-on-chronic liver failure, no such thing happens [right now]. That is why it is very critical for us to define: Where is the line in the sand?

Was there any notable disagreement about what direction you should go in, or what factors should be central to the definition?

We all were driven by the fact that our patients are currently being underserved by our differences. There were some groups which said perhaps we could further subdivide it into people who have no decompensation cirrhosis versus decompensated cirrhosis. There were also things about immune dysfunction and gut failure that were not completely resolved and were left for a future time.

But, by and large, the broad strokes about this were pretty much agreed upon. And what was especially exciting was we got input from the [U.S. Food and Drug Administration].

The FDA was, as always, very instructive because amongst the many groups that we had, one of them was clinical trial endpoints. They said, “This is not going to work. This may work for your local thing, but if you want to register an intervention, this is not going to be it.”

Have you gotten any feedback yet from pharma companies?

We got very good unofficial feedback from them. I think everyone is breathing a sigh of relief that at least now, we can move forward and come up with better ways to actually understand this condition, so that we can actually treat these patients better, develop therapies that can actually either prevent ACLF from progressing or mortality from improving, or at least lead them to a liver transplant before things become too late.

This document is huge, and there are a lot of statements. Is there anything else you want to highlight?

We benchmarked it to 30-day mortality across multiple consortia. So this was not based on consensus just because we like these cut-offs; we based it off of prior definitions, added twists to it, and then we saw whether this actually helped define 30-day mortality or not.

The most immediate impact is for us to move forward, and now start diagnosing and treating these people better. The second impact would be actually to train, to inform colleagues that are not within the liver world, who still deal with a lot of patients.

A majority of the countries and places do not have a hepatologist. They are dealing with GI people, hospital medicine, ER, critical care, or some other specialty. So the next step is to actually bring them on board, so that they are force amplifiers for this definition, and make sure that if someone reaches a very sick point, that they can actually be transferred very quickly to a liver transplant center.

#5712. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

#5710. California Passes Down Payment Assistance Plan, but Push To Cut Red Tape Remains in Limbo

California voters headed to the polls on Tuesday to decide three new housing-related ballot measures. While two of them handily passed, votes are still being counted on a plan to cut red tape and streamline environmental reviews for new homes.

Voters approved Proposition 1, which authorizes California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, permanent supportive housing, and affordable housing. The funding also backs both down payment assistance programs and mortgage programs for veterans.

Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed support for the measure, as did the Democratic Party of California. The ACLU, the California Apartment Association, and the California Housing Consortium also supported the measure, although there was some scattered opposition from Republican state legislators.

"This bond is about building communities, expanding access and affordability in California, where every family has a fair shot at a place to call home," Newsom said in a June statement.

Voters backed a similar measure in 2024 that earmarked $6.38 billion for homelessness and veterans housing programs.

"Higher mortgage rates have squeezed homebuyers and the for-sale market for four years, and they have hurt builders, too, especially in multifamily," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner says.

"Apartment projects depend on layers of financing, and assembling it has gotten much harder at today’s borrowing costs, particularly in a state as expensive and complicated to build in as California. When rates jumped in 2022 and 2023, a backlog of [COVID-19] pandemic-era projects that were already financed kept delivering homes. That backlog has been worked through, and the multifamily pipeline behind it is much thinner today," Berner adds.

Berner calls Prop 1 a "modest attempt to plug this gap" but only "one piece of the puzzle," noting that the infusion of cash won't do much to reduce approval times or land acquisition costs.

Californians also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income earners to purchase new homes. The state would issue bonds and use the proceeds to offer fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of newly constructed homes priced below $1.5 million

Borrowers must be California residents who pay at least 3% down and meet some income requirements. This, supporters say, would help lower the amount they'd need to save for a down payment on a new home. They expect the measure to spur the construction of new homes and be paid for when investors and home borrowers repay the loans.

The California Association of Realtors and the California Chamber of Commerce both supported the measure.

"Voters in California have seized the opportunity to help alleviate the burden of current mortgage rates on new-home buyers," says Berner of the initiative's passage. "With current mortgage rates holding above 7%, this presents the opportunity for buyers to save on interest payments for part of their home purchase, which could be a boon to the new-home segment of sales in the Golden State."

But, says Berner, housing is still above $1.5 million in many California metros, signaling that the measure's impact may be circumscribed.

"The median listing price for newly built single-family homes in the San Jose metro is over $2.1 million. In Los Angeles, it’s over $1.7 million. San Francisco has a median of about $1.5 million, and San Diego’s median is about $1.3 million. Among newly built single-family homes for sale in 2026 in the San Jose metro, just 41.7% were priced below $1.5 million. In Los Angeles, the share was 41.7% as well; 49.5% of newly built single-family homes in San Francisco were below the threshold; and in San Diego, 61.4% were. Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy."

Proposition 45 limits timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act. These new requirements would expedite environmental review and court challenges to projects.

Votes for the measure are still being counted. With 65% of the votes counted on Friday, 54.9% of Californians have voted against it while 45.1% voted in favor.

Affordable housing advocates—including the Associated General Contractors of California, the California Building Industry Association, the California Council for Affordable Housing, and the California Chamber of Commerce—expressed support for the measure.

Environmental groups and labor unions widely opposed it, arguing that it would reduce environmental oversight and community decision making around new development.

#5708. Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep

A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day.

Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression.

Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options.

Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia.

Major Review Finds Little Evidence of Sleep Benefits

To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia.

Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems.

Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning.

The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result.

There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement.

"The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population."

Why Scientists Remain Uncertain About Cannabis and Insomnia

One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted.

Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others.

The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use.

More Research Is Needed Before Cannabis Can Be Recommended

The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia.

Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions.

Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep.

Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence.

"The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated."

Novartis is largely abandoning an experimental drug analysts once considered a potential blockbuster after a study found it had little promise for preventing heart attacks and cardiovascular deaths, Bloomberg News notes. The move came as details of a key Novartis study were presented at the American Heart Association meeting this weekend. The growing field of research aimed at lipoprotein(a), a genetic risk factor for cardiovascular disease carried by 1 in 5 people, took a hit earlier this year when top-line Novartis results showed an experimental drug reduced Lp(a) but failed to lower serious outcomes. Other drugmakers pursuing Lp(a) drugs include Amgen, Eli Lilly, and Silence Therapeutics, STAT adds.

The Biotechnology Innovation Organization is joining the legal fight against a Trump administration pilot program aimed at aligning drug prices in Medicare with prices charged in peer countries, STAT says. BIO and two California-based biotech trade groups filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California asserting the Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing demonstration, known as GLOBE, oversteps Medicare’s statutory authority. The complaint seeks to halt the model. GLOBE, which applies to Medicare Part B drugs administered in doctor offices, is not expected to have much impact because the administration exempted all but a handful of companies in return for their agreement to voluntary deals to charge Medicaid most-favored-nation prices.

#5705. Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds

A major new study suggests that even modest amounts of alcohol may carry serious health consequences. Researchers found that drinking levels many Americans consider moderate are associated with higher risks of premature death, disability, cancer, heart disease, and other long-term health problems.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research challenges the longstanding belief that moderate drinking is harmless or may even provide health benefits. The findings suggest that alcohol's risks begin at relatively low levels of consumption and increase as people drink more.

"This study provides the most comprehensive U.S. estimates to date of lifetime risks of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity, showing that even moderate levels of consumption increase the risk of premature death and disability," said study co-author Katherine M. Keyes, PhD, professor of Epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

"No protective effect of drinking was observed even at low levels," added Keyes, whose research examines alcohol and other substance use across different stages of life.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," said lead study author Kevin Shield, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

Major Study Examines the Lifetime Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand how drinking affects health over a lifetime, researchers from the United States and Canada conducted an extensive review of existing scientific evidence.

Medical experts evaluated more than 7,200 scientific articles examining diseases and injuries associated with alcohol consumption. They used this evidence to determine how drinking influences the risk of individual health conditions, then combined those findings with large national health data sets.

Using statistical models, the team estimated how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious illnesses or dying prematurely over a lifetime.

The analysis covered a wide range of health problems linked to alcohol, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, injuries, and several forms of cancer. Among the cancers examined were those affecting the esophagus, mouth, and breast.

By considering these conditions together, the researchers were able to estimate alcohol's overall health burden rather than focusing on individual diseases.

Why Two Drinks a Day May Be Riskier Than You Think

One of the study's most important findings concerns drinking habits that many people would not consider excessive.

Consuming two alcoholic drinks per day, a level often viewed as socially moderate, was associated with a substantially higher risk of premature death attributable to alcohol.

The findings also provide more specific information than the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend that Americans "limit alcoholic beverages" but do not identify a particular amount that can be consumed safely.

Earlier dietary recommendations set daily limits of two alcoholic drinks for men and one for women. However, what counts as a single drink depends on the beverage and its alcohol content. A standard drink generally corresponds to 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits, although differences in alcohol concentration can change those amounts.

According to the researchers, the newer guidelines communicate a useful 'less-is-best' principle but lack specific numerical estimates that would help people understand how health risks change with consumption.

Their analysis was intended to fill that gap by measuring risks across a broad range of drinking levels.

Does Moderate Drinking Have Any Health Benefits?

For years, moderate alcohol consumption has sometimes been promoted as beneficial for cardiovascular health. The new findings cast doubt on that idea when the full range of alcohol-related health effects is considered.

The researchers found no statistically significant protective effect on overall health at any level of alcohol consumption.

They acknowledged that relatively low alcohol intake may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Ischemic heart disease occurs when reduced blood flow deprives the heart muscle of the oxygen it needs, often because arteries have narrowed or become blocked.

However, any potential cardiovascular benefits must be considered alongside alcohol's association with cancer, liver disease, injuries, and other serious conditions.

When the researchers combined these outcomes, the potential benefits were outweighed by the harmful effects, even among people consuming seven alcoholic drinks per week.

This broader assessment helps explain why a drinking habit that appears beneficial when examining one disease may still increase overall health risks.

Although the findings offer a clearer picture of the long-term dangers of alcohol, the researchers emphasize that the estimates describe risks across populations, not the precise likelihood that any individual will develop a particular disease.

The statistical models relied on "the best possible data," according to the research team. Nevertheless, personal health outcomes can differ considerably depending on genetics, lifestyle, drinking patterns, and other individual factors.

To calculate the overall burden of alcohol consumption, the investigators estimated risks for health conditions already known to have a causal relationship with drinking. They then combined those estimates to assess the total impact.

The researchers also acknowledged that scientific understanding of alcohol's health effects continues to evolve. Emerging evidence suggests that drinking may be associated with additional conditions, including pancreatic cancer, that require further investigation.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," said Keyes and Shield.

Despite these uncertainties, the results offer an important reference point: alcohol consumption above one drink per day was associated with increased health risks for both men and women.

The researchers believe that giving people more specific information about these risks can help them make better decisions about how much they drink.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking."

Why the Findings Matter for U.S. Alcohol Guidelines

The research also raises questions about how scientific evidence is considered when federal drinking recommendations are developed.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former associate administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, discussed the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the federal dietary guidance process.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Vincent's comments highlight concerns about whether the research received appropriate consideration during the development of national recommendations.

The study's findings reinforce the importance of understanding alcohol's cumulative health effects rather than assuming that moderate consumption is beneficial or risk-free. Although individual risks vary, the overall pattern was clear: greater alcohol consumption was associated with greater harm, and the researchers found no overall health advantage to drinking.

The research was funded by Synergy Enterprises Inc. and the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill Foundayo helped alleviate sleep apnea in two late-stage studies, but it doesn’t appear as effective as Lilly’s injectable drug Zepbound.

In a one-year trial of patients who weren’t receiving PAP therapy, a form of ventilation, those on Foundayo saw a reduction of 17.8 “events” per hour on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), a measure of the number of times breathing stops and becomes restricted while sleeping. #5703. Bear Grylls Bought a ‘Derelict’ Island With ‘No Power’ and ‘Rats’ at 25 Instead of a London Apartment—Here’s How It Looks Decades Later

Bear Grylls made an unusual decision decades ago, when he acquired a marital starter home with his wife, Shara Grylls.

“At 25, just married, we bought a small, abandoned, off-grid island from an ad in the back of a magazine,” the British adventurer, 52, wrote in a Nov. 3 Instagram caption.

Grylls revealed that the purchase of St. Tudwal’s Island West cost them around $120,000.

“There were many who thought us crazy,” he continued. “The best adventures start with nay-sayers. Thank you Shara for being brave and saying yes!”

While the comment section had users divided over the relatability of purchasing an entire island—with one commenter wondering how “celebrities get so far out of touch from reality and regular people”—there were also a handful of people who stepped in to point out that even when adjusted for inflation, the island was less costly than the average U.S. home.

The “Running Wild With Bear Grylls” star explained the decision to the Sunday Times in 2021, noting that snapping up a Welsh island seemed like a more exciting use of the couple’s money.

“In 2001, we were going to buy a London flat for $288,000, but we bought a houseboat on the Thames [now sold] and the island together, and it cost less than the apartment. So we decided on the path less trodden and an amazing adventure,” he said.

Grylls shed some light on just how dilapidated the property was 25 years ago.

“The island had a 200-year-old lighthouse and two lightkeeper’s cottages, but [the houses] were derelict with no power, no water, no roof, and rats,” he said. “I remember my first bath sitting in 3 inches of water pumped from the old tanks we’d cleaned out. There was rubble everywhere and rain coming through, but it was a great moment.”

Considering Grylls has made a career out of his ability to survive in extremely harsh conditions, it’s not entirely surprising that he was able to get through a few rough years before the island would become a more suitable dwelling.

It took a decade to get permission to build a slipway, which Grylls said they finished just a few years ago.

“It has been life-changing for us,” he said of the addition. “Previously we had to keep a boat on a mooring, row ashore, and walk a mile up the beach with all the shopping.”

Eventually, the two lightkeeper’s cottages were combined into a single home with four bedrooms. But the island is still off-grid.

“It’s 20 acres and 5 miles offshore with no mains, electricity, or running water,” Grylls told Vanity Fair in 2012. “It has a little lighthouse beside our house and is surrounded by amazing sea cliffs, seals, and dolphins. It is my favorite place on the planet!”

To travel to the destination, Grylls and his family take a “30-foot, high-speed ex-lifeboat,” which he described as a “rigid inflatable boat with twin 300-horsepower engines behind it that can tackle any sea it needs to.”

He said the house is “as tough as you get.” Thanks to “2-foot-thick old limestone walls,” it retains heat in the winter and stays cool in the summer.

“But when those gales come in, you can still feel it almost shake,” Grylls admitted. “Sea spray reaches the windows despite the 150-foot elevation.”

While St. Tudwal’s may lack some of the modern amenities guests might typically expect, the Grylls family does “sometimes have friends” visit.

“They need to be up for an adventure and prepared to get stuck there if the weather turns,” he said.

Grylls has recently made headlines for his connection to disgraced former comic Russell Brand, who was recently found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Grylls helped baptize Brand in a ceremony in the River Thames in 2024, after the allegations against the actor had come to light. Prior to the baptism, Brand appeared in a 2023 episode of Grylls’ show, in which the pair traveled across the Hebrides Islands.

“Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism,” Grylls wrote in a Nov. 6 X post. “I have attended a few now. Even visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes. It’s part of our calling as men and women of faith, to love and serve anyone. It is the sick that need healing.”

Noting that “judgment is for the courts and God,” Grylls added that “it is right that justice has now been served.

“I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day,” he said.

#5701. Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch

Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.

However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.

The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.

Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health

The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.

These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.

Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.

When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.

The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.

This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.

Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?

One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.

Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.

Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.

Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.

However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.

Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.

Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.

Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.

The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.

Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.

The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.

Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together

The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.

Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.

"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.

These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.

Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.

Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.
