#5645. Opendoor Says It ‘Rebuilt’ System With AI, Triples Home Purchases

After over a year of working as CEO, Opendoor’s Kaz Nejatian reported significant growth in revenue and market share during the iBuyer’s Q3 earnings call, and attributed the gains to a shift into AI infrastructure as the company says it has found ways to flip more homes without overpaying.

“This past quarter we rebuilt this entire system at Opendoor. We built an AI system that determines a specific repair plan for every single home before we buy it,” he stated. “Until August, our resale process was similar to literally everyone else in real estate. Pricing every home we owned basically lived in glorified spreadsheets with over 70 columns.”

As real estate incumbents have largely moved on from the iBuying craze that swept over the pandemic boom market, Opendoor has continued to push forward with a more nuanced approach to the model, offering a wider array of services to home sellers and partnerships with agents.

While acknowledging the company still has a long way to go, Nejatian is claiming the turnaround is working, even amid what he characterized as the worst years for housing “in a long time.”

“We’re winning the market without having to make riskier offers,” he said.

A lot of that comes from technology, along with a stronger focus on moving homes faster with less investment. Nejatian pointed out the differences between scaling with employees than with technology. He stated that increasing scale with the traditional method of buying homes involved hiring more employees, and a longer process.

“Rather than having people spending their days looking at pictures and doing mundane tasks, our people now each manage an army of agents,” he added. “In July, we had 5,400 homes. That’s 5,400 sellers sitting in a queue waiting for days for a human to confirm the price on their home. Two weeks ago, that queue was zero, and it will remain zero.”

He also homed in on the iBuyer’s new initiative—Buy with Opendoor—which launched in beta earlier this week. Although the Q3 earnings predates the program’s release, Opendoor CFO Christy Schwartz believes the initiative can open the company up to the broader market.

“Our emerging Buy with Opendoor offering can help buyers whether or not they’re buying a home from Opendoor,” she noted. “We see an opportunity to extend title and escrow to customers who aren’t buying or selling through Opendoor. Similar to listings, the offerings extend our reach beyond our home acquisition business and create opportunities to earn without taking ownership of a home.”

Previously, Nejatian came into the role with an aggressive turnaround mindset, touting an “Opendoor 2.0” initiative to bring the company back to significant profitability. The third quarter earnings may reflect the fruits of his labor, as homes purchased more than quadrupled.

“When a market slows down, companies are left with a cost structure and a system built for a different business. That’s the disease that Opendoor 2.0 is designed to cure,” he added. “That’s why I spend so much of my time on these calls talking about operator efficiency. When we say we’re investing in growth, we are building the capacity to handle the growth that will arrive.”

Overall, Opendoor’s third quarter saw a revenue of $1.02 billion, up 12% from last year’s revenue of $915 million and up 16% from the previous quarter of $883 million.

The number of homes purchased skyrocketed as well, increasing by 316% year-over-year from 1,169 in 2025 to 4,865 in 2026.

At the same time, though, Nejatian acknowledged the company is “behind schedule” on reaching profitability by the end of the year, blaming the slow market.

Opendoor’s stock fell sharply after the report, down about 17% at press time.

Again, Nejatian posited that the increases in efficiency with AI infrastructure have contributed to Q3’s results.

“Not that long ago, around 80% of the assessments we did on homes required an Opendoor employee, which could take many weeks. Today, that 80% is 2%,” he said. “In Q3, we purchased more than four times as many homes as a year ago, and our operation expense was basically the same.”

Operation expenses per acquired home fell to $4,000, down 36% from last year’s expenses of $6,300. The marketing expenses per acquired home dropped at a higher rate, down 57% to $2,800, compared to 2025’s $6,500.

Mortgage originations—or the process in which a borrower goes through to receive a home loan—increased over 400% from quarter-to-quarter, although the Q3 earnings may not reflect the full weight of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in mid-September. While the latest data does show mortgage rates inching down slowly each week, it’s unclear as to when rates will go below 7%.

“Historically, most of our economics have come from buying and reselling homes complimented by title and escrow,” Schwartz described. “Our emerging mortgage offerings allow us to earn more from each relationship while meeting a critical customer need and making the transaction easier.”

Opendoor’s EBITDA loss also improved slightly on a yearly basis. Q3 2026 had an EBITDA loss of $31 million, while last year had an EBITDA of $33 million. The adjusted EBITDA margin also decreased, now at 3% compared to last year’s margin of 3.6%. While better than last year, Schwartz acknowledged that the latest data is still far off from last quarter’s EBITDA loss of $4 million.

“Most of the sequential decline came from the homes we bought in the spring selling into a much weaker market along with deeper price cuts as we chose to clear rather than hold,” she said.

Looking to the future, Schwartz expects margins to decline again in the fourth quarter, and states that they will continue to sell through the remaining spring acquisitions into Q1 2027.

She also expects revenue to grow by at least 40% on a yearly basis in the next quarter. Although revenue may increase, Schwartz noted that marketing does contain a seasonal aspect, and operating expenses will likely increase due to investments and growth.

“Comparing year-over-year, roughly a third of the increase in our expected loss is the additional marketing, and the remaining two-thirds is primarily higher holding costs as we’ve been rebuilding our inventory,” she concluded.

“Our goal is to be adjusted net income positive on a 12-month-forward basis at the end of this year,” Nejatian continued. “We’re a bit behind on this today, but we’re going to go through some walls and catch up.”

#5644. Meet the 27-Year-Old Who’s Trying To Bring Housing Back to Rural Ohio

When it comes to the hottest locations that attract young 20-somethings, Mansfield, OH, probably isn't the first place that comes to mind.

For years, Mansfield’s nickname was “The Fun Center of Ohio” because of its family-friendly attractions and its status in the 1970s as a mini-bike manufacturing hub.

More recently, the town of 47,000, located halfway between Columbus and Cleveland, earned the local nickname of “Danger City” after the Westinghouse electric plant left in 1990 and the town fell into deep economic decline.

The 27-year-old serial entrepreneur, who started a painting and landscaping business as a teenager, relocated to Mansfield from Seattle a year ago, hoping to revitalize rural housing through his vertically integrated housing development company, Western Dominion Land.

Vertical integration is a development model in which a single company controls the full life cycle of a housing project.

“In other countries, they’ve figured out that vertically integrating construction means you’re not paying a margin out to every single step," Goehner explains. "If you own the system—from a lumberyard, to producing panels or modular, to buying the land, to developing the land, to building the homes—you're not paying everyone’s markup along the way, and you can actually deliver that home at a reasonable price.”

Goehner is building a factory in Mansfield to produce structured panels that he says will cut single-family home construction from months to weeks and allow him to charge much less than other builders. The first panels are expected to roll off the production line in early 2027.

Currently, it takes 8.8 months to construct a home from start to finish, according to the National Association of Home Builders. Goehner says his process allows a home to be built and move-in-ready in 40 days.

Western Dominion has already built about 500 housing units across Ohio, starting at $200,000 for a single-family home.

Western Dominion focuses on what it calls "attainable housing"—homes priced below what the median household income in the area can afford but not income-limited, meaning they work for the vast majority of families and buyers.

In Mansfield, where the median listing price is $229,000, he says, "single-family homes at $215,000 sold instantly. At $260,000, they sat for months."

As he sees it, 25% of the homes on the market are priced for 60% to 70% of buyers, while the rest of what’s being built is at the top end of the market. Furthermore, only 8% of construction happens in rural areas, despite 20% of the population living there.

"The government is too focused on low-income housing" and low-income housing tax credits, he says. “And the last few housing bills they passed were only structured to deliver essentially more urban multifamily units and incentivize builders to build more low-income housing with tax credits."

In rural communities, he adds, “We have a terrible amount of aged housing inventory. Most of our homes are from before 1970, which would be fine if it didn't cost so much to remodel.

“From the '90s to the 2000s, we’re building a good amount of homes. As a country, we were doing about 1.6 million a year. And then in rural America, we were doing about 220,000 homes a year. And then 2008 hits, and that drops down to about 60,000 homes a year in rural America."

Along the way, smaller builders disappeared, and larger builders were disincentivized from building in rural areas because of the red tape involved.

"If you want to build in rural America and you go to a bank, unless you have all the cash, you have to show comps," he says. "You've got to be, like, ‘All right, we think these homes are going to sell for this much because these guys sold for this much.' And if no one's built for five to 50 years, which is the case in a lot of these communities, that can be difficult."

The added costs of building in rural areas, like having to pull utilities, "mean you're spending $25,000 to $50,000 per lot before you can even start putting a house on it or connecting your utilities to the lot."

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, home prices in rural communities have risen sharply. A Realtor.com® housing analysis of home prices from November 2019 to November 2025 found that median listing prices increased more than 70% in rural counties while in-metro counties saw home prices increase around 30% during the same time period.

"A lot of the politicians we talk to, they go, 'I didn't know that that county needed housing. I didn't know rural needed housing because the population is shrinking.' But then when you look at why the population is shrinking, it's because they haven't gotten any new homes for 20 to 40 years."

"You've got this huge demand. But on paper, on the surface, it looks like there's no demand because the population's declining," he continues. "And that's how you get cities like Holiday City."

Holiday City, near the Ohio border with Indiana and Michigan, has a population of just 48 people, but it is home to three large businesses—Chase Brass & Copper Co., 20/20 Custom Molded Products, and a Menards Distribution Center—which draw around 1,500 commuters from out of state.

"Let's put up, you know, 300 homes, and a portion of the workforce can actually stop commuting an hour or two every day," Goehner says.

Goehner hopes Ohio's new slate of elected officials will help advance rural building by offsetting some of the infrastructure-related costs of building in rural areas. In exchange, he would sell homes at his “attainable” housing rates.

"The government needs to stop spending thousands of dollars a month per unit to subsidize rents when they could simply spend a little bit upfront to make it viable to build at a reasonable price point again," he says.

#5642. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.

#5641. A Rare $7M Double Townhome Hits the Market in DC—Complete With a Heated Terrace and ‘Fortress’ Garage

The word "compound" is very rarely associated with townhouses in bustling city neighborhoods, but a $7 million property in Washington DC’s Dupont Circle might just be the exception.

Offered together, the connected luxury residences at 1617 and 1619 19th Street NW are an incredibly rare opportunity to own some serious square footage in one of the capital’s most vibrant areas.

The property is anchored by 1619—a four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom residence that spans four impeccably-renovated levels. Next door, 1617 serves as a complementary rowhome with three fully-leased residences—a spacious one bedroom with a private patio, and two additional two-bedroom, two-bathroom units.

Spanning 6,600 square feet and boasting nine bedrooms and 9.5 half-bathrooms between them, the pair of buildings has "all kinds of unique use cases," according to listing agent Barak Sky with Serhant.

Sky explains that there are plenty of impressive features that could make this the perfect situation for a "needle in a haystack buyer who can’t find exactly what they need."

Perhaps a notable public figure would like to reside in the four-level residence, and dedicate one of the smaller units in the secondary building to a round-the-clock security team. A family could take advantage of the opportunity to create a multigenerational home.

Maybe it’s just right for a buyer who wants to live in a gorgeous home and generate rental income. The three units currently pull in $136,200 annually, according to the listing.

“It’s definitely special,” says Sky. “We thought this was a unique opportunity to present this compound as one offering.”

Aside from the fact that the sheer volume of space is ripe with possibility, there’s another feature of the property that brings endless potential.

“The detached garage is completely like a fortress,” Sky adds.

A steel two-car garage is structurally engineered for future expansion, and could be used to add a private, elevated pool deck or even an additional accessory residence. Given the historic nature of the property, which was built in 1910, the chance to add to the building’s legacy is certainly exciting.

Should the buyer choose to leave everything as-is, they’re still in for a treat.

The primary residence has been painstakingly renovated, and features an “uncompromising commitment to craftsmanship,” according to the listing, which touts the dwelling’s “soaring ceilings and extensive custom millwork.”

A private elevator services each floor, connecting the sprawling formal spaces, gourmet kitchen, and inviting family room to the private retreats upstairs.

An entire level is dedicated to the primary suite, which includes a private terrace, dual walk-in closets, and a spa-inspired marble bathroom equipped with heated floors, a steam shower, and a sauna.

Of the additional bedrooms, two are ensuites.

The lower level hosts a recreation lounge, a temperature-controlled wine cellar, a guest suite, and space for what could become an efficiency kitchen.

The outdoor space is just as lavish, and is described as a “spectacular private sanctuary” in the listing. There’s a wood-burning fireplace, outdoor audio and television, heat lamps for the winter, a misting system for the summer, and heated walkways.

There are also a number of seemingly invisible amenities that were carefully selected to make life more comfortable, such as seamlessly-integrated smart home technology and whole-house water filtration.

As for the location, this gem is located on one of Dupont Circle’s "most coveted tree-lined blocks,”"according to the listing.

“This exceptional offering places the very best of Washington at your doorstep, from acclaimed restaurants, boutique shopping, and neighborhood cafes to Embassy Row, downtown business districts, cultural institutions, and Metro access,” it reads.

#5640. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5639. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5638. Two Neighboring $9.9 Million Oceanfront Homes Just Listed in Kauai’s South Shore—And They Can Form an Ultra-Luxe Compound

Tucked into a private-club community in Hawaii called Kukui‘ula, two luxury homes just hit the market on Kauai's South Shore.

Set right on the ocean, and set among lush tropical vegetation, this walkable community is only 25-minute drive from Lihue Airport.

"The close proximity of everything is very convenient. You’re not having to spend a lot of time in the car,” says Pancho Sullivan of Hawaii Life, who is co-listing the two homes with Haunani Sullivan as well as Suzanne Harding and Jeff Skinner of Kukui‘ula Realty Group. The asking price sits at $9,900,000 each.

Both were built in 2025 and have never been occupied. Aepo Nei 18 and Aepo Nei 19 are neighboring 3,372-square-foot homes with four bedrooms and 4.5 baths each. They can be purchased together, to create a private compound, or by separate buyers.

Even better, the homes are fully furnished and stocked with items like bed and bath linens, beach towels, and everything you need to cook and serve in the kitchen, such as bowls, plates and glasses.

But it’s the design by Brazil-based Architects+CO that’s truly unique. Kauai Bahia Construction and their in-house material company, Kayu, handled all of the finish material production and millwork installation.

"Brazil is known for incredible resort-club communities," says Pancho. "We actually traveled to Brazil to look at some of the clubs they designed. It’s the same tropical feel (as Hawaii) that blends in really well with nature."

Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions while Aepo Nei 19’s living spaces open onto a lawn courtyard. Design features at both include deep roof overhangs, walls of glass and multiple outdoor living spaces such as an infinity-edge pool; jacuzzi; swim-in, swim-out sauna; and in-water fire pit.

"They both have beautiful 180-degree ocean views looking across the Tom Weiskopf-designed golf course. The swim-in, swim-out dry sauna facing the ocean is a unique feature," says Pancho, adding that the usage of natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak "fit into the landscape very beautifully."

Referred to as the Garden Island, Kauai is home to about 73,000 people.

"We get the majority of the island’s sunshine down here," says Haunani, about the South Shore. "People flock here for the beaches and the sunshine, Hawaiian monk seals on the sand, and a lot of ocean activity including surfing.

"A lot of people that venture to Kauai are adventure seekers. We have great hiking. You can get on a boat and dive on the Nā Pali Coast and do ziplining and ATV tours."

Stand-up paddleboarding, diving and fishing are two other activities easy to do in this community.

Homeowners become club members with access to dining, a pool, spa (boasting a steam rook and lava-rock dry sauna), pickleball and tennis courts, and an 18-hole golf course.

"There’s an incredible gym with classes daily, from yoga to sound bathing to fitness training," says Pancho. "All of that is part of your club membership. It’s a great place to be in tune with nature and get healthy."

A 10-acre organic garden features a farm stand as well as opportunities to create floral bouquets. There’s also a conscious effort to honor Hawaiian history through cultural-heritage walks; sunrise ceremonies; hula performances; and classes in Hawaiian featherwork, quilting and basket weaving.

“Members who are part of the club become life-long friends,” says Haunani. “They’re going to each other’s second homes and weddings. They travel around the world together.”

The community also organizes annual golf and pickleball tournaments for members, and three golf courses are within a seven-minute drive.

Another incentive is that the community’s zoned as a Vacation Destination Area.

This means properties can join the short-term rental pool, for minimum seven-night stays.

"Some of the owners put their homes in the rental pool and block out time for themselves and their families. That’s a great added benefit," says Haunani, as few club communities on Kauai allow this.

The Sullivans think the buyer will likely hail from the West Coast, enticed by a direct flight from hubs in cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix and Denver that arrive on the island by mid-day.

“Kukui‘ula is a great place for families to gather and spend time together. We see a lot of members bring their entire families so they can vacation together multiple times per year,” says Pancho.

“With all these activities it’s easy to curate an incredible vacation with the convenience of being on property. A lot of people enjoy coming here and decompressing.”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5636. Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B

Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a deal valued at $5.3 billion.

The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.

Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.

The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.

Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.

Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.

According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team.

Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.

The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.

Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.

Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.

#5635. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5634. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5633. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5632. Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features

Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million.

The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX Agent Cloud, a service that artificial intelligence agents can use to store their data. Dropbox is also adding new AI productivity features to its flagship file sharing platform.

Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris Data offers an object storage service that runs across multiple public clouds. The company says that it enables applications to read and write several times faster than competing offerings. Furthermore, the service includes several features designed to optimize AI workloads.

AI agents often run in sandboxes that include, among other resources, the data they need to carry out their work. Loading data into a sandbox can be a relatively time-consuming process, which slows agent performance. Tigris Data offers a feature called bucket forms that speeds up the workflow. Furthermore, it prevents agents from modifying information that is used by other workloads.

Tigris Data’s service monitors the locations from which agents access records. When it detects a new location, it moves a copy of the records to a nearby server in order to reduce latency. The service caches the most frequently used files on high-speed storage infrastructure to further reduce access times.

Dropbox said Tigris Data will support its push into the AI infrastructure market. The company debuted its first entry into that product category, DBX Agent Cloud, in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Like Tigris Data’s service, it’s an S3-compatible object storage offering optimized for AI agents.

The storage stalwart plans to add a file system capability further down the line. Object storage is best suited for unstructured datasets, while file systems are used to store records that are organized into folders. Dropbox plans to release the technology alongside “content processing capabilities.” The company says that those features will make it easier for AI models to process information kept in DBX Agent Cloud.

The offering is rolling out alongside a major overhaul of Dropbox’s flagship file sharing platform. An enhanced search bar will enable users to look for images by entering a description of the file they seek.

Furthermore, Dropbox can now respond to questions about a file by generating a natural language summary. A worker could, for example, request an overview of the changes that colleagues have made to an important folder over the past week.

Dropbox can not only edit questions about files but also edit them. The company says that users can have the built-in AI models change a file’s format, move it to a different folder or combine it with other records into a PDF document. Several other actions are supported as well. Users can mix and match actions into multistep workflows.

The new AI productivity features are initially available to customers in the U.S., the U.K. and Australia with Standard and Advanced subscriptions. Dropbox plans to expand access next year.

#5631. Housing Week Ahead: Hottest Markets, Inflation, and Existing-Home Sales

The coming week brings a steady stream of new reports from the Realtor.com economics team, as well as a number of key indicators for the housing market.

On Monday, senior economist Anthony Smith published the October Luxury Report, which looks at pockets of growth where luxury prices are still rising.

On Tuesday, ahead of Veterans Day, we honor America’s military service members and veterans with a report on Veterans Affairs loans. Senior economist Jiayi Xu explores what they are and how they help with homeownership.

On Wednesday, senior economist Hannah Jones examines how the lock-in effect has evolved and where today’s homeowners with a mortgage face larger or smaller payment shocks if they are thinking about moving.

On Thursday, Hannah is back to examine what the first full week of November data reveals about the housing market, and on Friday, Hannah publishes the October Hottest Markets report, which identifies the markets where homes are moving the fastest and getting the most attention from online shoppers.

Turning to the economic indicators that will be released, we’ll see the consumer price index reading on inflation as well as mortgage rates and existing-home sales.

Inflation has run above the Fed’s target, 2% growth in headline PCE, for 5.5 years, and it’s clear from exit polls that the cost of living was very much on the mind of voters in last week’s election.

This week, we’ll see the first inflation reading for October from the consumer price index, which was up sharply in September largely due to higher energy prices. I’m expecting the annual inflation reading to be similarly high in October even if the month-to-month momentum wanes a bit.

Although inflation remains elevated, mortgage rates could continue to ebb. Last week the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, according to Freddie Mac, dropped to 7.18% as the 10-year hovered near 4.9%.

Late in the week, the 10-year yield dropped further as uncertainty over artificial intelligence investments led to a pullback in stocks. Even if the 10-year were to remain at 4.9%, it has adjusted faster than mortgage rates, so I think there is room for spread compression that could help nudge rates lower, which will help late-season home shoppers.

The last indicator of the week is existing-home sales data from the National Association of Realtors®. That October home sales data is likely to be very disappointing.

Mortgage rates rose sharply in the month, and NAR’s pending home sales hit a series record low in September, while Realtor.com housing data suggests that the buyer pullback continued into October. I’m watching to see if the pullback is sufficient to push months supply even higher.

For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research.

Danielle Hale is the chief economist of Realtor.com.

#5629. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.
