#5613. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5612. Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but will Big Tech end up winning anyway?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?

The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.

Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer.

And the AI juggernaut indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.

All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.

Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time. We can walk and chew gum at the same time if we put our mind to it. Hard to imagine the Dems could do worse than Trump and the GOP have been doing for years now.

#5611. Donna Kelce Sells Florida Condo for $485K—Less Than a Year After Major Makeover

NFL matriarch Donna Kelce has offloaded her newly renovated Florida condo for $485,000—less than a year after carrying out a complete overhaul of the pad.

In March, it was revealed that the 74-year-old mother of NFL stars Travis and Jason Kelce had embarked on a major overhaul of her Orlando abode, hiring a local company to replace multiple windows and doors throughout the two-bedroom property.

The project sparked an over-the-top response from fans of the famous football family, and led to Donna's sons calling out the reaction in an episode of their podcast, "New Heights," during which they mocked their mother over the work, joking that she was attempting to turn her condo into a "gilded palace."

However, the renovations seemed to make a big difference when it came to selling the home, with TMZ reporting that the property has found a new owner.

Donna has owned the 1,434-square-foot property since 2019, when she purchased the residence for $355,000. The condo, which was built in 2005, features a wraparound balcony, a den, library, home office, and workout room.

The mom of two previously spoke out about the renovation in a candid interview with Architectural Digest, telling the outlet that work was completed on her home—while setting the record straight about the changes that were made to the dwelling.

"It’s a lot of windows because I’m on the side of the building. So there’s like 16 windows, and they’re floor-length, and it was quite a project," she shared, before hitting back at reports that she'd needed to replace six doors during the renovation.

"The windows that are floor-length along the balcony, they call all of them doors, but they weren’t," she stated. "There were only two doors. But there were six of those [in total], and two of them had handles on them."

As for the viral response to her renovation news, Donna admitted that it "took [her] by surprise," adding: "I was kind of taken off guard."

At the time, Donna revealed she was looking forward to relaxing inside the updated space, explaining that she's happily settled into her routine in the property, where she lives alone, having divorced her former spouse, Ed, soon after their sons finished college.

Addressing her daily routine at home, the proud grandma said she begins each day with coffee, before figuring out what's on her agenda—and confirming whether or not it will require her to go to the airport.

Her children are also a big priority, she said, noting that, while they are both "so busy, it's almost impossible" to speak to them every day, she does her best to check in as often as she can.

"Especially in the offseason, I have no idea what city they’re in [or] where they’re going. But they’re always on my mind," she said.

She admitted that much of her relaxation time revolves around her favorite gadget in the house—her television—which she regularly eats her meals in front of, noting that she "doesn't really care what anybody thinks" about her habits, particularly because she lives alone.

"It connects you to the world. It allows you to relax. Not only that, but it’s important to have to learn about the news and what’s going on in the world," she added.

Donna said she will occasionally fall asleep with the TV on, but sets a timer to ensure that she isn't snoozing in front of the screen for longer than 20 minutes.

And while she seems fairly relaxed about her life at home, the mother of two admitted that she does have one very clear rule for guests who visit: no pets allowed on the furniture.

"I don’t have any pets. I think a person’s home is their home, and if that’s where they want their pet, have at it. If it’s in my house, no. But most people that I know of who have animals allow their pets on the furniture," she explained.

In addition to being a place Donna can relax, she said her condo was also packed with precious reminders of her sons' success—and the incredible experiences she has enjoyed as a result of their hard work.

“There are so many [photos]. So many pictures of all the amazing people that I've been able to meet, all the wonderful places that I've been able to go, all the games, all the Super Bowls,” Donna shared.

“It's more than a mother should ever hope for. I can't even tell you how full of love and admiration [I am] for my kids to be able to give that to our family.”

Donna's dwelling first shot into the headlines back in March, when TMZ revealed that she was carrying out construction work at the home. Her sons then added further fuel to the fire when they raised it as a topic of conversation on "New Heights."

Addressing the furor surrounding the renovations on their podcast that same week, Travis and Jason joked to their listeners: "Let's talk about the most important news out of the Kelce family this week. We wanted to break this news on the show, but reports have already started to leak out."

"Donna Kelce is remodeling her modest Florida home! Let's give it up for Donna!" Jason added.

The siblings then brought Donna in to share her thoughts on the media response to her renovation plans—with the NFL matriarch admitting that she had been stunned by the attention it received.

"Even TMZ sent me a text and said, 'Can you be honest, it's really funny!' I'm like ... it's so stupid!" she said, before attempting to play down the work she's having done.

"All they're doing is, people are coming to put in my windows on Monday," she continued. "You know my whole apartment is all windows. It's windows all the way around."

Still, Jason couldn't help but get in another joke, asking: "Are you going to bulletproof?"

Undeterred, Donna continued by explaining that the unseasonably cold weather in Orlando had motivated her to replace the existing window designs, because they were "cheap" and outdated, providing little protection against the chill.

"This year, it got so cold down here—it was in the 30s—and I literally had sweat coming down the windows and pools of water in my living room because it couldn't handle it. These are cheap windows that were put in 20 years ago," she shared.

Jason then called out TMZ's description of Donna's property as a "modest home," joking that she appears to have plans to turn it into a much swankier abode.

"Well, I just wanted to say, 'Mom, they said "modest home," and it just feels like you're turning this place into a bit of a gilded palace,'" he said.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5610. For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.

Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier.

Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard.

Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data.

A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers.

The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers.

Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers.

The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month.

Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas, where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale.

While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.”

The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market.

The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer’s market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes

The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months.

House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas.

But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s  market may offer an opportunity.

“Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova, a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said.

Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova.

For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said.

Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs.

Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier.

The typical condo that sold in September spent 63 days on the market before going under contract, up from 35 days five years earlier.

Condo buyers in Texas had more negotiating powers than anywhere else in the country in September. San Antonio had the widest seller-buyer gap among the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas, with an estimated 459% more sellers than buyers. Houston followed with 322% more sellers than buyers, then came Austin, with 258% more.

Miami also had one of the nation’s widest gaps, with an estimated 274% more condo sellers than buyers in September, ranking third.

“San Antonio condos may have an attractive purchase price, but buyers are looking at the total monthly payment. Because we have so many affordable single-family homes available, many buyers choose a house when the payments are close,” said Derrell Skillman, a Redfin Premier agent in San Antonio, TX.

Skillman added San Antonio has a large military community, and its housing market tends to follow the military’s permanent change-of-station (PCS) season.

“We usually see more military-related activity during the spring and summer when families are transferring in and out of the area. Once that period slows down, the drop in demand can be more noticeable, especially in a smaller segment like condos,” he said. “HOA costs, financing restrictions, builder incentives, softer investor demand and the slowdown after the military PCS season are all contributing to the buyer’s market for condos,” said Skillman.

Meanwhile, new construction is adding to the softness in Sun Belt markets. The Sun Belt is home to nine of the 10 metros where condo sellers outnumber buyers most.

Nassau County, NY, was the only metro area among the 50 analyzed that was a seller’s market for condos in September. There were 32% fewer sellers than buyers, with an estimated 1,545 buyers compared with 1,052 sellers.

“Condo buyers are mostly people who want maintenance-free living,” said William Ortiz, a Redfin Premier agent in Long Island, NY. “They want to have an easier lifestyle as opposed to all the maintenance and upkeep that comes with a house. Common charges are expensive, but they’re willing to pay for that convenience.”

According to Sandra Glaser, a Redfin senior agent in Long Island, condo demand is coming from three main groups: first-time buyers priced out of single-family homes, particularly those moving from the city to the suburbs; downsizers seeking less upkeep; and investors looking for rental income from properties that require minimal maintenance.

Five other metros — Chicago, Milwaukee, New Brunswick, Newark and San Francisco — had balanced condo markets, where the difference between buyers and sellers was within 10%.

San Francisco’s condo market, for example, is heating up, with the median sale price jumping 20% year over year to nearly $1.2 million in September. Khan, the Redfin senior economist, ties the area’s renewed housing demand to the AI boom, which is attracting highly paid workers and fueling homebuying.

As a senior data reporter, Dian uses data and quantitative analysis to tell stories about economy and real estate. She also builds databases and creates statistical charts that visualize data trends. Previously, Dian spent seven years as a senior data reporter at USA TODAY.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5609. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5608. Mortgage Mix: Buyers Turning to ARMs Due to Elevated Rates; Compass Expands Its Mortgage Business

Editor’s Note: The Mortgage Mix is RISMedia’s highlight reel of need-to-know mortgage-industry happenings. Watch for it every other Friday afternoon.

The numbers: While mortgage rates had hit a peak and were nearing the high-end of the 7% range, they have now decreased for the third straight week to 7.18% for the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage and 6.57% for the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage. Notably, this was the lowest level seen in over a month.

What this means: A stronger jobs report was partially attributed to this week’s improvement, as Realtor.com® Senior Economist Hannah Jones said that “while solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term.

The “blue wave” that occurred in the elections this past Tuesday may also contribute to further improvements down the road, as Jones noted that “many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead.”

Using their ARMs? Despite a come down, many buyers are still holding off from the market due to rates remaining over 7%. Mortgage applications this week were down 1.2%.

With the fixed-rate mortgage elevated, more buyers have turned to adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) instead.

“As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025,” said Mike Fratantoni, the Mortgage Bankers Association’s SVP and chief economist.

A Better battle comes to an end: After a tumultuous struggle between the lender and its founder, Better.com has dropped its federal securities lawsuit against Vishal Garg, who was ousted in August. The case was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

The lender had been suing Garg for allegedly violating federal securities laws, arguing that he did not engage in the proper process to solicit shareholders in a bid to regain his position.

That bid ended up being successful, with Garg back in a leadership role.

Compass takes mortgage JV to the big leagues: Expanding its mortgage business to become a top-10 lender, Compass announced a merger between its own OriginPoint mortgage platform and Rate’s Guaranteed Rate Affinity to unite the two mortgage ventures under the OriginPoint brand.

Guaranteed Rate Affinity was founded in partnership with Anywhere Real Estate back in 2017, making the merger an unsurprising move due to Compass’s acquisition of Anywhere last year.

The merger expands OriginPoint’s resources and geographic reach, the companies noted in a release, while backing the business with Rate’s AI technology, products and lending platform.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5607. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5606. Russell Brand Moved to Florida Months Before British Police Formally Charged Him With Rape

British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to over 10 years behind bars—more than a year after he relocated his entire family to Florida to escape "attacks" by the "media, government, and judiciary."

According to the New York Times, a London court found Brand, 51—who was previously married to pop star Katy Perry, and now shares three children with wife Laura Brand—guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and not guilty of two additional counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," Judge Joel Bennathan said while handing down the sentence in a London court on Nov. 9.

Following an April 2025 arrest by Metropolitan Police, Brand denied all charges, sharing a video statement on his X account, in which he insisted that he has "never engaged in non-consensual activity," while conceding that he had acted like "a fool" when he was "young and single."

"I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family, who were just about a shot over there, my beautiful children, I was a fool, man," he said in the video, which appears to have been shot in Florida.

The alleged offenses are understood to involve six women and took place between 1999 and 2009. Police interviewed Brand about the allegations—which were first brought to light in 2023, when The Sunday Times and Channel 4, two British media outlets, released an expose in which Brand's accusers claimed they had been assaulted or raped by the comedian.

Brand vehemently denied all accusations of "non-consensual activity" at the time.

He is understood to have moved his family from their home in Oxfordshire in favor of a rental property in the Sunshine State, where he is reportedly living in a $2.5 million home in Santa Rosa Beach.

Although he has not revealed when exactly he moved, it has been reported by multiple outlets that he relocated shortly before the 2024 presidential election. Images taken of the comedian show him enjoying public events in the Santa Rosa Beach area as early as October of that year.

The Times reported in 2025 that Brand, his wife, and their three children had been living in a $3.3 million home in the U.K. before their move. It is unclear if they have since sold it.

Brand has also not confirmed whether he is planning to purchase a home in the U.S., where he is currently renting a property.

In the lead-up to his move, the comedian and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" star had been making efforts to connect with members of now-President Donald Trump's inner circle, interviewing Donald Trump Jr. at his Florida home in 2024 and attending a black-tie dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where he received a Global Defender of Freedom Award.

In April 2025, Brand sat down for an in-depth interview with Fox News host—and newly minted Florida resident—Sean Hannity, during which he opened up about his past addictions and his Christian faith.

Since moving to Santa Rosa Beach, the comedian has reportedly been seen attending church services, as well as yoga sessions, with one local telling The Sun that Brand "always says hello" when they see him.

It is not the first time that Brand has resided in the U.S., having previously owned multiple properties in Los Angeles—including a $6.5 million Mediterranean-style home in the Hollywood Hills, which he shared with Perry, his wife at the time.

Before that, he was reported to have been living in a 1920s abode nearby, which he purchased for $2.2 million in 2013.

Most recently, he snapped up a three-bedroom, five-bathroom Spanish-style property, also in the Hollywood Hills, this time paying $3 million.

The home, which Brand bought in 2019, was built in 1956. The original listing noted that it had since undergone several renovations. He put that property on the market for $3.5 million in summer 2024.

Charlie Lankston is the executive editor at Realtor.com. She previously worked at DailyMail.com as the associate editor covering news, celebrities, travel, lifestyle, and the British royals. In 2019, she was part of the DailyMailTV team that won a Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Entertainment News Program. Charlie earned a B.A. in English literature and theatre studies from the University of Warwick and an M.A. in newspaper journalism from City University in London. Originally from London, she has been based in New York City for 12 years.

#5605. AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.

To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc,, who has some deep experience in this area.

As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.

She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.

When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family: Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.

The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:

The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AWS Supply Chain was such a useful learning experience. When Aubrey got close to the product, she saw a team working to catch up rather than lead. They had been building five modules that “largely were about getting to feature parity” with entrenched enterprise resource planning vendors that had a decades-long head start.

Connect had taken the opposite path, and it’s instructive. “They understood they weren’t going to achieve feature parity,” Aubrey said of the Connect team. Instead, they led with outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone, started narrow and built from there.

Aubrey applied that same lesson to the supply chain. She rebooted it as Connect Decisions by asking a different question: where is the pain most acute, and where is the current tooling weakest? The answer was planners. “They’re firefighting the whole time,” she said. “They’re overwhelmed by a whole bunch of signals. By the time they get to decide, the moment has passed.”

The same applies to enterprises. AI projects that stall often try to replicate an entire workflow. The ones that succeed identify a painful decision point and make it dramatically better.

Aubrey’s point about measurement deserves unpacking. “Companies are stuck on what’s the ROI of AI, and they’re looking at return on tokens and this sort of stuff,” she said. “The question is, can you move your business metrics by working in a different way?”

Her proof point is Wells Vehicle Electronics, which, according to AWS, cut inventory by 7% in three months while expanding the SKUs they actively monitor from 20 to 2,000. Nobody at Wells is talking about tokens. They’re talking about working capital. If a project can’t be tied to a metric the chief financial officer already tracks, it’s an experiment, not an investment.

Amazon started where most companies start: with software development, making AI tools available across the company. Aubrey admits there’s a bit of chaos at first. “Everyone’s just experimenting with a bunch of things,” Aubrey said.

She sees that as a feature, not a bug, because that’s where the real learning happens. “You go through this learning period of, you know what, our test coverage sucks,” she said. Fix test coverage, and you find “our pipelines suck,” so you fix pipeline health, eliminate manual intervention and deploy faster. The result in her group this year: a twofold improvement in the velocity of pushes to production.

The lesson is that the velocity didn’t come from the coding assistant. It came from fixing everything downstream that the assistant exposed. Enterprises that buy the tool and skip the plumbing will see activity rise while output stays flat.

I asked Aubrey whether Amazon has adjusted its goals to reflect what employees can now do with AI. Her answer was an honest “yes and no.” In her user experience team, roles have collapsed: designers are being pushed to ship code to an alpha environment, and Amazon has created a new “UX tech” role.

The “no” is that org design and goal-setting are still catching up. Her message to her team is blunt: “The only choice you can’t make is to own the task. You have to choose to own the outcome.” Every IT leader should borrow that line. Task-based job descriptions will age poorly.

AWS’s design philosophy for the Connect family is what she calls “humorphism,” the idea that AI should fit the way people already work, not the other way around. Her biggest concern is the lag between internal prototypes and production.

“Shipping good AI with a bad user experience will fail, in my opinion,” she said. Her team has invested heavily in closing that gap, moving beyond traditional command-based interfaces toward AI that picks up cues, remembers decisions, and carries work forward. The goal, she said, is to make AI so usable that people change how they work, not because they’re told to, but because it makes sense.

She was equally candid about maturity. TE Connectivity has scaled Connect Decisions to 2,000 planners, but Connect Talent reached general availability only in September and has early customers in deployment. Aubrey said the team is focused on getting the product right before aggressively scaling, reflecting the same “pick a wedge” discipline she applied across the Connect solutions.

What made this conversation valuable was Aubrey’s willingness to share how she thinks about building AI products that work in production, from studying what made Connect successful to applying those lessons across supply chain, hiring, health care, and customer engagement. That candor is a useful model for IT leaders, because most enterprise AI programs are stuck for the same reasons AWS’s applications once were: too much breadth, too little focus and success measured by the wrong yardstick.

The AI era won’t reward companies with the most pilots. It will reward those that pick a sharp problem, fix the plumbing it exposes, redesign work around outcomes and move the metrics they already have.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5603. Japan spent a record $50 billion in a single day to prop up the yen

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tokyo bought 15.4 trillion yen over three days from July 30, including a joint operation with the U.S. on July 31

Japan committed a record 7.98 trillion yen (about $50 billion) on July 30 alone to shore up its currency, according to Ministry of Finance data released Monday.

The ministry’s quarterly figures showed that Tokyo stepped into the market on three separate days. It committed 5.55 trillion yen on July 31, then a further 1.87 trillion on Aug. 3, according to Reuters. The combined 15.4 trillion yen bought across those sessions makes it the largest yen-buying episode Japan has mounted, according to The Japan Times.

The July 30 outlay beat the prior one-day high of 6.28 trillion yen from April 30, in a ministry data series that starts in 1991, according to Reuters. The three-day total also came in higher than Japan's outlays during April and May, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The three-day breakdown surprised the market, because traders had assumed the intervention was confined to two sessions, according to The Japan Times.

The U.S. took part in the July 31 operation by selling euros for yen, according to Reuters. It was the first time since 1998 that Japan and the U.S. had worked in concert to lift the yen's value, according to The Japan Times.

Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the coordinated intervention, according to The Wall Street Journal. Bessent addressed the yen's decline candidly over the summer and endorsed Tokyo's moves to push back against the currency's undervaluation.

The yen had fallen to near 164 per dollar, its weakest level in 40 years, when Japan re-entered the market on July 30, according to Reuters.

The Bank of Japan lifted its benchmark rate to 1.25% in September, and another increase is anticipated before the year closes, according to The Wall Street Journal. The central bank has pointed to the weak yen as a significant consideration in its projections for the economy and inflation.

#5601. CoreWeave is asking Texas's incoming governor to work with it on data centers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CoreWeave offered to help finish permitted projects and set standards for new ones after Hinojosa won on a data center moratorium pledge

CoreWeave wrote to Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa to propose collaborating with her incoming team on data center projects both underway and still being planned, according to Bloomberg.

CoreWeave co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Michael Intrator offered to work with Hinojosa's transition team to see already-permitted projects through and to establish standards for later buildouts. "You have made clear that data center growth must work for Texas," Intrator said, according to Bloomberg. "We strongly support those principles."

Hinojosa became the first Democrat to capture the Texas governorship since 1990, according to Bloomberg. Her campaign promise was a statewide moratorium on data centers, and she has since sketched out ways to pair stiffer regulation with the state’s business-friendly reputation, Bloomberg said. “We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans,” Hinojosa said in an interview on Thursday, according to Bloomberg.

Carl Holshouser, who runs government affairs at CoreWeave, wrote in a LinkedIn post that Hinojosa had made it plain that projects already holding permits can be finished, according to The Next Web. The Next Web found no record of Hinojosa making that claim in her own words, and her team has not explained how a pause would be carried out.

Holshouser, who co-wrote the letter, said the cost of building new transmission lines and generating plants should not fall on families, and that new sites need to safeguard local water and electricity supplies, according to The Next Web.

CoreWeave's bonds tumbled on Wednesday after Hinojosa won the governor's race on a pledge to halt data center development. CoreWeave stock fell 9.9% that day to close at $48.42, its weakest finish since May 2025.

A CoreWeave spokesperson said in a statement that the company does not anticipate any impact to existing customer commitments or associated backlog from shifts in the political landscape. Republicans hold the majority in the Texas Legislature, which limits how much Hinojosa can change state policy.

#5600. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5599. Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa.

Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs.

Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. The company plans to release the model’s weights under an open-source license next week.

#5598. Johnson & Johnson is backing a psychedelic-inspired depression startup in a $100 million round

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Delix Therapeutics plans to start a placebo-controlled Phase II trial of its depression pill zalsupindole in the first half of 2027

Johnson & Johnson $JNJ led a $100 million Series C financing in Delix Therapeutics, a Bedford, Massachusetts, developer of psychedelic-inspired depression treatments, the company said on Monday. J&J invested through its venture capital arm, Johnson & Johnson Innovation – JJDC.

SV Health Investors' Dementia Discovery Fund co-led the round. Existing investors including RA Capital, UC Investments and Artis Ventures took part, as did new investors including Adage Capital Management and Hamilton Square $SQ Partners Management, Delix said.

The money will fund Phase II development of Delix's lead drug, zalsupindole, in recurrent major depressive disorder, along with the company's other neuroplastogen programs, the company said. Delix expects to start the placebo-controlled Phase II trial in the first half of 2027.

The trial will enroll 240 patients, who will be dosed either every day or two times a week for a month, according to Bloomberg. Data should arrive in the first half of 2028, Bloomberg said.

Zalsupindole is an oral compound inspired by 5-MeO-DMT and designed to promote neuroplasticity without hallucinations, Delix said. In a Phase Ib trial in adults with recurrent major depressive disorder, patients had a mean reduction of about 50% in depression scores after one week of treatment. The improvement held through day 36, four weeks after the final dose.

That study involved 18 patients, and a bigger trial that includes a placebo group will be needed to verify the findings, according to Bloomberg.

"This capital enables us to take Zalsupindole through Phase II Proof of Concept," Delix CEO Mark Rus said in a statement.

Christian Jung, a partner at SV Health Investors, and a JJDC representative have joined Delix's board, the company said.

Delix has taken in $115 million across previous financings but would not share what the company is worth, according to Bloomberg. Rus told Bloomberg the company intends to look into an initial public offering next year, though that hinges on how markets behave and how its clinical work goes.

The financing follows other big-company moves into psychedelic medicine. Eli Lilly $LLY agreed in July to acquire AtaiBeckley, a developer of psychedelic-based mental health treatments, for roughly $2.8 billion in cash, with up to roughly $1 billion more tied to development and regulatory milestones.

The FDA also held a public hearing in September on the therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, where speakers called for clear safety and access standards.
