#5597. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5596. Charter is cutting $2 billion in costs as internet subscriber losses worsen

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Charter posted a $2.4 billion third-quarter net loss tied to a $6.3 billion franchise impairment charge, versus a profit a year earlier

Charter Communications announced a new operating model on Friday that aims to trim $2 billion from its yearly cost base, measured on an annualized run-rate basis, within the next 18 months.

The savings are in addition to more than $1 billion in anticipated synergies from the Cox Communications transactions, the company said. The program will target nonessential activities for removal, streamline how the organization is structured and capture efficiencies by working more closely with vendors.

Charter lost 233,000 internet customers on a pro forma basis in the third quarter, compared with a loss of 171,000 in the year-earlier quarter. Legacy Charter lost 156,000 internet customers, versus 109,000 a year earlier, and legacy Cox lost 77,000. Charter served 34.3 million internet customers as of Sept. 30.

"We are fundamentally rethinking how we operate and compete," Chris Winfrey, Charter's president and CEO, said in a statement. Winfrey said Charter intends to bring back growth in its internet customer base while turning into a leaner, quicker and more nimble company.

Charter is also reformulating its go-to-market approach for its core internet offering, marketing and distribution, the company said.

Charter reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $2.4 billion, or $20.50 a share, for the third quarter. It had net income of $1.1 billion a year earlier. The company attributed the loss to a $6.3 billion franchise impairment charge, offset in part by a $1.4 billion gain on extinguishment of debt.

Revenue rose 9.1% to $14.9 billion, driven by the Cox transactions. Pro forma results treat the Cox deal as if it closed on Jan. 1, 2024. On that basis, revenue fell 1.5% to $16.5 billion, and adjusted EBITDA fell 4.0% to $6.6 billion.

Charter added 508,000 mobile lines on a pro forma basis. Video customers fell by 77,000, compared with a decline of 121,000 a year earlier. Charter stock dropped 7% to $117.04 ahead of the market open Friday.

Competition from rivals offering fixed-wireless and fiber service has eroded the base of households subscribing to Charter's internet, while the shift toward streaming has undercut its cable operations, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Charter completed its acquisition of Cox Communications in August. The deal added more than 11 million passings and over 5 million customer relationships, according to the company. On Sept. 16, Charter launched Spectrum's products, pricing and packaging across the legacy Cox footprint.

#5595. Edgevana Signs $700 Million in AI Infrastructure Agreements as Committed Demand Reaches $7 Billion

With more than $20 billion in active pipeline, the company supporting the largest hyperscalers in the world will deploy NVIDIA Blackwell systems across North America and Europe.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Edgevana, the data center, energy and compute orchestration platform delivering production-ready AI compute, today announced more than $700 million in fully committed, multi-year take-or-pay agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell computing systems across North America and Europe. The commitment comes as power constraints delay traditional data center builds, driving $7 billion in contracted customer demand and an active pipeline exceeding $20 billion for Edgevana's pre-energized platform.

Under the agreements, Edgevana will orchestrate and deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs and GB300 systems across North America and Europe. By unifying pre-energized land, data center facilities, and high-speed networks into a single virtual campus, Edgevana enables customers to bring tens of megawatts of high-density AI compute online in 90-120 days. This allows enterprises to bypass years of greenfield build delays while retaining single-pane control over their distributed compute footprint.

"We stayed in stealth through the initial training boom on purpose, and in many ways, we still operate that way because our model isn't obvious to the broader market," said Ryan Fay, Co-CEO of Edgevana. "Training rewards centralized megaâcampuses, but inference is live production traffic. As performance demands increase, it plays directly into our core strengths. We cut our teeth delivering ultra-low latency for high-frequency trading and managing edge production for two of the world's largest hyperscalers. Now that AI is pivoting to inference, the market has come to us."

Edgevana's global network spans 17 operational data center locations, with another 10 in active development. Collectively, the platforms powered by Edgevana's infrastructure serve over 10,000 downstream enterprise customers, most of whose users never realize Edgevana is the layer making it possible.

"The defining constraint on AI isn't algorithms or software, it's physical, heavy-duty infrastructure," said Subhan Jahromi, Co-CEO of Edgevana. "While the market focused exclusively on mega-gigawatt campuses, we spent years quietly securing the power, land, and compute required to bring infrastructure closer to the end user. Getting high-performance GPUs to the edge reliably and at scale is incredibly difficult. As our name suggests, Edgevana makes edge deployment seamless.

Edgevana builds and combines long-term energy supply, its unique GPU allocation, and committed customer demand into a capital-efficient deployment model. By securing long-term contracts ahead of deployment, Edgevana reduces financial risk, accelerates time to compute, and delivers dedicated AI capacity at a lower cost basis than traditional providers.

About Edgevana:Founded in 2019, Edgevana is a globally distributed AI compute company accelerating the deployment of next-generation AI infrastructure. Powering the world's leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, Edgevana delivers high-performance AI clusters at unprecedented speed and scale. By unifying power, data centers, GPU infrastructure, and connectivity through a single platform, Edgevana dramatically reduces time to value, enabling AI labs and enterprises to deploy dedicated compute capacity in months rather than years. Through strategic access to power, infrastructure, and advanced compute, Edgevana delivers the speed, scale, and economics required to power the AI revolution. Together, Edgevana is powering the ideas that power the world. Learn more at edgevana.com.

#5594. OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation

OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as sources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today.

The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.

It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.

Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal, one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.

The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well.

The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing.

In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending.

Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving.

#5593. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5591. BYD unveiled a $310,000 electric sedan to rival Rolls-Royce

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Yangwang opened China reservations for a limited edition at a preliminary 2.08 million yuan; sales elsewhere are not announced

BYD’s luxury brand Yangwang unveiled the Altior, an all-electric four-seat sedan, at a global premiere in Abu Dhabi, the company said. The car uses four motors and has a range of more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) on the CLTC cycle.

The Nov. 7 event marked the first time the brand had staged a worldwide premiere beyond China, according to TechNode. Yangwang opened reservations for a limited edition with a preliminary price of 2.08 million yuan, about $311,000, and a deposit of 300,000 yuan.

The Altior measures 5.6 meters (18.4 feet) long, 2.03 meters (6.7 feet) wide and 1.59 meters (5.2 feet) tall, with a 3.5-meter (11.5-foot) wheelbase, BYD said. Its four motors are each controlled separately, which lets the car fine-tune the torque sent to every wheel over 100 times every second. The car can perform tank turns and has an emergency flotation function for accidental entry into water.

BYD said the car uses its Second-Generation Blade Battery and supports FLASH Charging. Additional technical details and charging specifications will be announced at a later date, the company said.

Inside, the rear seats are aviation-style zero-gravity seats with massage systems. The cabin has a 39-speaker Dynaudio sound system, a powered 21.4-inch overhead screen, and front and rear refrigerators. Yellow Hetian jade finishes the air vents, and the upholstery features both Suzhou embroidery and perforated sections. Front doors open to 80 degrees and rear doors to 90 degrees.

The Altior will come in Executive and Bespoke editions, BYD said. The first themed Bespoke Edition, Shanhe Dingyun, has a brown and gold exterior and a jade-inspired interior. BYD said it will be a limited run.

Design Director Wolfgang Egger said in a statement that the design draws on the ding, an ancient Chinese ceremonial bronze vessel, and took three years to develop. "ALTIOR represents our vision for the future of Chinese luxury," BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said in a statement.

The car targets sedans from Rolls-Royce, Bentley and Mercedes-Maybach, according to Carscoops. A Rolls-Royce Phantom starts at roughly 8.5 million yuan in China. BYD has not announced availability outside China.

The launch follows BYD's push into overseas markets. BYD reported second-quarter net profit of 8.2 billion yuan, up 30% from a year earlier. First-half exports rose 71% to more than 790,000 vehicles, or 44% of total sales.

#5589. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5588. KKR posted record quarterly profit as fee-related earnings climbed 27%

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Assets under management rose 11% to $804 billion, and KKR expects to return more than $40 billion to clients in 2026

KKR reported record adjusted net income per share of $1.78 for the third quarter on Monday as fee-related earnings rose 27% from a year earlier to $1.3 billion.

The adjusted figure beat analyst estimates of $1.58 per share, according to The Wall Street Journal, and of $1.59, according to Reuters.

Adjusted net income rose 29% to $1.6 billion. Total operating earnings climbed 25% to $1.7 billion. For the second consecutive quarter, KKR posted record fee-related earnings, total operating earnings and adjusted net income per share.

Management fees rose to $1.20 billion from $1.06 billion a year earlier. Fee-related performance revenues rose to $326 million from $73 million.

Net income attributable to common stockholders totaled $1.12 billion, equal to $1.19 per diluted share, up from $859.9 million, which worked out to 90 cents per share, in the year-earlier period. Total revenue dropped to $4.56 billion from $5.53 billion. Insurance revenue declined to $2.80 billion from $3.78 billion.

"We continue to monetize investments and return capital to our clients at record levels," Co-CEOs Joseph Bae and Scott Nuttall said in a statement, according to Reuters. KKR anticipates distributing over $40 billion back to clients in 2026, which would top its prior annual high by more than 50%.

Assets under management rose 11% from a year earlier to $804 billion. Fee-paying assets under management also rose 11%, to $648 billion. KKR brought in $25 billion of fresh capital in the quarter and deployed $20 billion.

Insurance operating earnings were $230 million, down from $305 million a year earlier. The latest figure included a $26 million charge tied to Global Atlantic's annual actuarial assumption review and related items. The year-earlier figure included a $41 million benefit from the same review.

KKR announced the sale of USI Insurance Services on Aug. 31. The deal is expected to be completed during the fourth quarter. Subject to closing, KKR expects it to generate about $2.0 billion of adjusted net income, or more than $2.00 per share, in the fourth quarter. The company said there is no assurance the transaction will be completed.

From June 30 through Nov. 4, KKR used $567 million to repurchase and retire 6.2 million shares at an average price of $92. On Nov. 6, it approved a $500 million increase to its share repurchase program. KKR declared a quarterly dividend of $0.195 per share, payable Dec. 3 to holders of record on Nov. 19.

KKR will hold a conference call on the results at 10 a.m. ET on Monday.

#5587. National Safety Council Expands Tools to Help Employers Make the Business Case for Life-Saving Technology

Work to Zero calculators help employers quantify the costs, savings and potential return on investments to prevent serious incidents and fatalities

WASHINGTON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As employers look to technology to prevent serious workplace incidents and fatalities, one question can stand in the way of adoption: How do you demonstrate the value of the investment? The National Safety Council is helping employers answer that question with an expanded suite of free Employer Investment Calculators that allow businesses to estimate the financial impact and return on investment of safety technologies using their own operational data.

Developed through the NSC Work to Zero program in partnership with McElhattan Foundation, the enhanced calculator suite has expanded from eight to 13 technologies, including EHS software, heat stress monitoring and ergonomics video analytics. Approximately 8,500 users annually already use the calculators to evaluate potential safety investments.

The need for better investment decisions is particularly urgent when it comes to preventing the most serious workplace incidents. Although the Occupational Safety and Health Administration recordable injury rate has declined significantly over the past 25 years, workplace fatalities have not fallen at the same pace. More than 4,500 workers died on the job in 2023. Beyond the human toll, workplace injuries carry significant financial costs. The average medically consulted injury costs an estimated $43,000 and the average workplace fatality costs $1.46 million.

"Too often, employers know a safety technology could save lives but struggle to demonstrate its business value," said Dr. Matt Law, director of Work to Zero at NSC. "These expanded investment calculators help organizations quantify the financial impact of preventing serious incidents and fatalities. By making it easier to build a strong business case, we can accelerate the adoption of technologies that protect workers and ultimately save lives."

Employers can use the calculators to compare technology costs with potential savings, test different scenarios and estimate a five-year return on investment. The expanded suite of calculators reflects the growing range of solutions employers are adopting to reduce workplace risks.

The accompanying report, Making the Business Case for Safety Innovation, outlines a five-step framework for evaluating safety technology investments â from assessing organizational readiness and identifying appropriate solutions to calculating ROI and securing leadership buy-in. It also explains how the calculators compare the costs of maintaining current risk levels against the potential savings from reducing serious injuries and fatalities.

Together, the report and calculators give safety leaders a practical pathway from identifying a workplace risk to evaluating a technology solution, demonstrating its value and building the case for adoption.

Work to Zero is part of the Council's ongoing effort to eliminate workplace fatalities through the advancement and adoption of technology-based safety solutions. To access the calculators, report and additional resources to create safer workplaces, visit nsc.org/worktozero. To register for the Building the Business Case for Safety Technology webinar, visit here.

#5586. AI cyber resilience and the trust gap

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante and Krista Case

Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets.

In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake?

Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit.

Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes.

Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments.

We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions:

These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require.

Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI.

Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested.

These findings come from a small sample of in-depth interviews conducted with our partner Qualitate. The conversations allowed us to explore what customers have tested, the additional security work their own AI creates and what it takes to resume a business process safely. One healthcare practitioner phrased the disconnect between confidence and readiness as follows:

No, we have not completed any tabletop exercises as it pertains to an AI agent or other similar attacks. We’re highly confident because these are scenarios similar to non-AI incidents we have handled before.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Across the interviews, respondents who did express confidence often drew heavily on existing ransomware and incident response playbooks. Their experience with non-AI incidents understandably provides a degree of trust. But it also raises a concern in that organizations may assume that an agent taking an incorrect action can be handled in the same way as an insider or external attacker doing something similar. We don’t believe existing playbooks cover all scenarios.

Rather, we believe that assumption needs to be tested against the specific demands of an agent incident. The interviews revealed a mixed picture of true validation:

Complete business recovery requires an organization to reconstruct a sequence of authorized actions, identify incorrect outcomes, repair downstream effects and safely resume the affected business process. Demonstrating that the full sequence works is a nontrivial exercise.

The speed, scale and interconnected nature of agent activity makes that even more challenging. Actions can affect multiple systems and processes, creating consequences that existing playbooks need to account for. We see a risk of false confidence when organizations assume that their experience with traditional non-AI incidents will translate automatically. Testing needs to establish how well their capabilities hold up under the conditions an agent can create, which may be novel.

Bottom line: Evidence of validated, end-to-end business recovery from an agent incident remains limited in our study. We believe organizations should exercise their existing playbooks against realistic agent scenarios, with safe business resumption as the measure of success.

Our interviews raised questions about tooling, maturity and the processes needed to prove that existing capabilities work for agentic AI. Two findings as shown below highlight the limited reach of detection and reconstruction capabilities in the organizations studied:

One healthcare practitioner’s assessment of the controls already implemented underscores the trust gap:

No, for the ones that have been implemented, we have not tested or validated that they work.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Enterprises already have identity systems, application logs, data protection tools and the like, along with established incident response processes. They are trying to extend these capabilities to AI. The central challenge is validating that the tools can reconstruct activity across an entire agent workflow.

Agents interact with multiple applications, invoke tools and autonomously trigger downstream actions. Each system may capture its own events without providing a coherent record of the complete workflow. Incident response requires correlating those records to establish which agent acted and under what authority, then tracing the tools it invoked and the changes that resulted.

This reminds us of the early days of disaster recovery, when organizations would test failover but hesitate to test failback because they were nervous about what might happen. We see a similar reluctance to ask questions that could expose gaps in readiness or cause downstream problems. The concern is whether the connected tools and processes will hold up under realistic agent incident conditions.

Bottom line: Organizations need to exercise the full agent workflow under realistic conditions, including a plausible worst-case event, and validate that their tools and processes can reconstruct the activity and support the response.

Our assessment of the field interviews highlights both the technical and business dimensions involved in a recovery. An AI agent can use legitimate access to change a record incorrectly or send a message that should never have been sent. A backup may work and the restored systems may appear healthy while the business remains unable to resume safely.

StorageTek veteran Fred Moore, an early mentor to Dave Vellante, coined the phrase: “Backup is one thing, recovery is everything.” The scope of recovery continues to expand as organizations consider the consequences of agents acting across business systems.

A director of information security at a media and entertainment firm described the problem this way:

We could restore our systems, we could restore within our recovery objectives, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that it’s safe. The bottleneck here would be trust.

— Director of information security, media and entertainment

Recovery point objectives or RPO and recovery time objectives or RTO are the so-called business metrics. But business users need more meaningful key performance indicators that resonate — specifically, what a trusted, viable service looks like and how that condition can be verified. That includes establishing who needs to participate in recovery and who signs off that operations can safely resume.

This direction needs to come from the top down; and be verified bottom up. Business leaders must define the requirements, with IT and security acting as partners to provide the underlying technology and help achieve the required outcome. The responsibility extends beyond the traditional data protection team’s work of recovering data and systems.

Incorrect transactions, human error and failures that ripple across systems have existed for a long time. Agentic AI adds two complications:

That requires a comprehensive view of what went wrong and what needs to happen to recover. The organization must be able to trace the agent’s activity and evaluate the resulting business state against clear criteria for safe operation.

Bottom line: Recovery requires explicit criteria for verifying that a business service can be trusted and clear responsibility for approving its return to operation. The business must set that direction, with IT and security providing the capabilities to carry it out.

Humans in the loop help organizations restrict what agents can do. Resilience also has to account for what happens when a human misses an incorrect action or cannot keep pace with agents operating at machine speed. Two statements from the same CIO illustrates the issue:

So the given scenario will be detected by human beings before the AI agents can take the actions.

If it really happens, currently we do not have the capability to roll back the agent’s action.

— Chief information officer, real estate and construction

The first statement shows confidence that human oversight will catch the problem. The second acknowledges a missing “undo command” if the human oversight fails. This captures why approvals and recovery testing need to advance together. Reliance on human intervention can bring a false sense of security and defer attention to the recovery details needed when a mistake gets through.

Our field study also revealed how customers are weighing the tradeoffs around autonomy, with organizations generally still containing what their agents can do. Those decisions become particularly important when agents receive authority to take remedial actions during an incident or recovery.

The level of autonomy granted should reflect the risk of the action. Before allowing an agent to approve or execute a remedial action, organizations need to understand the consequences of an incorrect decision. That calls for a tiered approach built around two considerations:

We expect human approval to become an increasingly significant bottleneck over the next six to 12 months. Organizations need to establish these boundaries as they begin trusting agents to take more remedial actions.

Bottom line: Human oversight and recovery testing need to develop together. As organizations delegate more authority to agents, they must account for mistakes, the limits of human review and the risk associated with each action.

A retail practitioner described a viable approach to rehearsing an agent incident and we see this as a best practice. Specifically, this firm replays the agent’s actions in a replica environment, investigating the root cause and using granular snapshots to understand the transactional effects. The respondent explicitly confirmed that the approach had been tested in the sandbox with the following statement:

Yes, if the agent went across multiple systems, my approach is to replay this within my sandbox environment, which is a full replica of all of the systems.

— Director of information technology, retail

The value of this approach is in reproducing the sequence of events and investigating their effects across systems. Our assessment of what such an exercise should confirm is anchored on three outcomes:

We see these as minimum viable expectations for the evidence an exercise should produce.

We use the term digital twin here as a broad analogy for this approach. A fuller digital twin would involve a richer representation of business processes, dependencies and state. We believe the industry still has work to do in that direction, and that work will become more important as enterprises use AI to run critical functions. In addition, it will further expand the notion of recovery as the state of the business will become increasingly more complicated as agents perform more of the work.

The respondent also acknowledged a limitation saying: larger transaction volumes could require more time for reconciliation. Replaying actions and identifying affected transactions provides useful information, while the time needed to resolve their consequences remains an open item. Richer simulations of business environments could help organizations test agent behavior and prepare for what a failure might look like in production.

In other words, testing the recovery sequence in a variety of scenarios inside a digital twin of the business prior to pushing the process into production. Further, this “red teaming” exercise must be ongoing – expanding the concept of continuous data protection into the state of a firm’s operations in more granular snapshots.

Bottom line: This example offers a practical approach to reproducing agent actions, investigating their consequences and rehearsing recovery. Its value also points toward the need for richer representations of the business processes those agents affect.

If a chief information security officer takes one action from this study, we recommend exercising an agent incident affecting one consequential workflow already in production. Choose a workflow in which an agent has permission to act across multiple systems, and design the exercise to include incorrect actions taken with valid credentials and permissions.

The exercise should also include a scenario requiring human approval. This helps establish the boundaries around where autonomy is appropriate and where human oversight remains necessary.

Validation by the business owner is essential. Security teams can establish that an incident has been contained and provide evidence of what happened. The business owner must determine whether the resulting business state is acceptable. That decision needs to account for the consequences of the agent’s actions and any remediation work still required.

The exercise should document what was proved, what remains untested and which teams are responsible for closing the remaining gaps. That evidence should also inform decisions about how much authority an agent receives. The organization needs to understand its ability to reverse or correct actions and recover their consequences as it considers granting greater autonomy.

The discussions at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit reinforced the themes emerging from the field study. Conversations with vendors, practitioners and researchers underscored the need to build resilience and recovery into agent deployments from the outset. Evidence that these capabilities work becomes essential as agentic workloads move into production.

The challenge includes preserving and recovering a trusted business state when an agent produces an incorrect outcome despite having legitimate credentials. Organizations need to understand how those outcomes affect their operations and what it will take to address them.

Existing investments in data protection infrastructure, security and recovery remain critical. The work ahead is to identify the gaps that emerge under the new requirements and pressures created by enterprise AI. That requires collaboration across internal teams and with vendors to understand where capabilities need to improve.

Bottom line: We believe trust in enterprise AI requires tested evidence that organizations can understand what agents have done, stop them, reconstruct their actions and recover to a healthy business state. Our research indicates that organizations still have work to do to demonstrate that their existing security and recovery capabilities can meet that requirement.

#5585. Vanguard is extending proxy voting choice to all its U.S. equity funds

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Investor Choice expansion covers $8.2 trillion in assets, including the world's largest mutual fund, and starts next year

Vanguard Group is expanding its Investor Choice proxy voting program to all of its U.S. equity funds, according to Bloomberg. The funds hold $8.2 trillion in assets, and the change takes effect next year.

Investors in the funds will get to decide which voting approach is applied to their stakes, according to Bloomberg. The expansion covers the Vanguard Total Stock Market Index Fund, which Bloomberg describes as the world’s largest mutual fund.

Clients who sign up can choose from proxy voting policies that fit their views, among them backing company management or emphasizing environmental, social and governance goals, according to Bloomberg. That choice sets the way their slice of the fund is voted at shareholder meetings of publicly traded companies, on matters such as director elections, compensation for executives and central ESG issues. In most cases, the pass-through system stops short of giving a single investor control over how their stake is cast on each separate ballot question.

Vanguard has offered Investor Choice to clients since 2023, according to Bloomberg. The latest update doubles the amount of assets the program covers.

John Galloway, Vanguard's global head of investor engagement, said the program can help address any worry that a fund company's votes lean toward a particular bias, according to Bloomberg. He added that the firm engages with policymakers.

"We have over 50 million individual investors in the U.S., and tens of millions more internationally; those individuals have a wide range of perspectives," Galloway told Bloomberg. He said participation in the program shows investor views fall across the spectrum, in what he called a normal distribution.

Vanguard joins other large U.S. asset managers, including BlackRock $BLK and State Street $STT, that have introduced proxy voting programs, according to Bloomberg. The firms argue that these programs widen investor options and capture the variety of views among their clients. The growth of pass-through voting has coincided with greater U.S. political scrutiny of how far money managers back proposals tied to ESG goals.

#5584. Conexiant and Elsevier Announce Licensing Agreement for The Lancet: Research in Context

New specialty-focused initiative connects healthcare professionals with globally authoritative research, advance clinical understanding, and creates trusted engagement opportunities across 10 therapeutic areas

TAMPA, Fla. and LONDON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Conexiant and Elsevier announced a licensing agreement naming Conexiant as a commercial licensing partner for The Lancet: Research in Context, a digital initiative designed to extend the reach of context-rich in the Lancet journals and connect it with relevant healthcare professional and life sciences audiences. The program launched last week across 10 therapeutic areas

Research in Context is a core feature of primary research journals in the Lancet Group. It helps readers understand the evidence that existed before a study, the added value of the new findings, and the implications of the full body of evidence for clinical practice, policy, and future research.

Conexiant and Elsevier expand access to The Lancet research across 10 therapeutic areas through a licensing agreement.

The initiative features dedicated, therapeutic area-specific digital destinations and related e-newsletters and engagement programs built around Research in Context content. By organizing globally authoritative research around key disease states, the experiences help clinicians more quickly interpret important findings while maintaining a clear path back to the original Lancet articles. This approach was designed to deepen healthcare professional engagement, increase discoverability of source research, and support informed clinical decision-making.

The first phase includes non-small cell lung cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers, follicular lymphoma, multiple myeloma, gynecologic cancers, renal cell carcinoma, Alzheimer's disease, and inflammatory bowel disease. The platform provides a scalable framework for future expansion and support greater visibility for Lancet research among clinicians, researchers, authors, reviewers, and industry audiences worldwide.

The program includes a trusted, highly contextual environment for life sciences engagement around some of medicine's most actively researched therapeutic areas. Future opportunities may include support for calls for papers, peer reviewer recruitment, and other programs that strengthen connections across the global research community.

"This partnership represents another exciting step in our relationship with Elsevier and reflects exactly where we believe medical publishing is headed," said Charlie Lee, Chief Executive Officer of Conexiant. "By extending access to The Lancet: Research in Context content, we can help life sciences organizations engage in a more meaningful way around the clinical topics that matter most, while always driving healthcare professionals back to the original source content."

"Research in Context has long been an important part of how Lancet journals help readers understand new findings in light of existing evidence," said Laura Hassink, Managing Director of Elsevier Journals. "Through this new licensing relationship with Conexiant, we are creating an additional pathway for that context-rich content to reach relevant specialized audiences, deepen engagement with Lancet research, and maintain a clear connection back to the original published articles."

The agreement expands the existing relationship between Conexiant and Elsevier and builds on their previously announced work in society marketing and member engagement. Both organizations view the initiative as an opportunity to develop new models for contextual scientific communication, clinical innovation, audience engagement, and licensed dissemination built around trusted medical content.

Research in Context is a core feature of primary research articles across the Lancet family. It is designed to help readers understand the evidence that existed before the study, the added value of the new findings, and the implications of the full body of evidence for practice, policy, and future research. The Lancet editors introduced the concept for clinical trials in 2005 and later expanded the requirement across Lancet journals in 2015.

Conexiant is a global healthcare media, education, and engagement network that connects trusted clinical knowledge with the healthcare professionals who put it into practice. Through long-standing relationships with more than 190 medical societies, health systems, publishers, and life sciences organizations, Conexiant combines global authority, specialty expertise, editorial depth, digital solutions, events, learning, publications, and commercial capabilities to deepen HCP engagement, advance clinical innovation, and support better clinical decisions. For more information, visit www.conexiant.com.

Elsevier is a global leader in advanced information and decision support that helps advance science and healthcare. Elsevier serves academic and corporate research communities, clinicians, educators, and future healthcare professionals worldwide and is part of RELX, a global provider of information-based analytics and decision tools for professional and business customers.

#5583. WeatherBug Ushers in a New Season for Weather Apps With a Radically Helpful New Forecasting Experience

Reimagined app and website make personalized weather easier to understand, turning complex data into clear, actionable insights for everyday life

NEW YORK, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Americans are constantly checking the forecast. Nearly three-quarters of Americans 1 (73%) check the weather at least once a day, and a whopping 90% say the weather impacts their mood, plans or routines, according to a new WeatherBug survey conducted by The Harris Poll.

But for all the weather information at our fingertips, the forecast doesn't always make the next decision easier. More than half of weather app users (53%) say they're often unsure whether to change their plans after checking their weather app, while 39% say their weather app alerts often feel more stressful than helpful. The problem isn't a lack of weather data. It's understanding what that data means for your day.

Today, the sun is rising on a new day for weather apps. WeatherBug unveils the biggest evolution of its digital experience in 15 years, with a completely reimagined app and website designed to make local weather easier to understand, faster to navigate and more useful in the everyday moments that matter most.

"Rather than simply putting more meteorological information in front of people, we designed the new WeatherBug to put the forecast into context and make it more useful in everyday life," said Gundeep Hora, President of WeatherBug. "Checking the weather is really just the beginning. People want to know: How close is that storm to my house? Is the air quality good enough for my run? Should I grab an umbrella on my way out? WeatherBug humanizes the forecasting experience, offering clearer guidance for whatever the day has in store."

The update represents a major evolution for WeatherBug as it shifts from a traditional weather data provider toward a more human-centered weather companion.

Taking the Guesswork Out of the ForecastAt the heart of the new experience is a simple idea: less decoding, more understanding.

The redesigned home screen puts the hourly forecast front and center, while simplified navigation makes key features easier to access. Across the app and website, major weather experiences have also been upgraded.

From Data to DecisionsTogether, these advancements reflect a broader shift in the weather forecasting category, spearheaded by WeatherBug.

"People don't necessarily need another number, chart or alert. They need to understand how the weather may impact their day," said Zeeshan Khan, Head of Product Design at WeatherBug. "We put data into context, whether that means understanding pollen levels in your neighborhood, knowing when outdoor conditions will improve or putting today's temperature in perspective. It's about moving from simply forecasting what the weather will be to helping people understand how it will impact their day."

After 30 years of helping people keep an eye on the sky, WeatherBug is looking toward the next season of weather forecasting, with the core belief that understanding the forecast is just as important as seeing it.

Available on iOS and Android, with a web experience at WeatherBug.com. WeatherBug holds a 4.8-star rating based on more than 2.2 million ratings on the Apple App Store, making it one of the most recommended and trusted weather brands.
