#5582. Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?

The October jobs report showed 165,000 payroll growth and a steady 4.1% unemployment rate, consistent with improved 2026 labor conditions. Yield direction was driven more by AI-related market swings and broader bond market levels, keeping mortgage rates near 7.17%.  AI Summary

With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well.

Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement.

From BLS:  Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing.The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed’s is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year.

Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it’s still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor.

This month’s report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad.

Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline?

One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet.

As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave’s stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break.

Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That’s good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today’s episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler.

A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows.

#5581. McDonald's is making Uber its preferred delivery partner in 14 countries

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The multi-year deal gives Uber precedence over DoorDash for McDonald's app orders and adds Uber ride discounts to MyMcDonald's Rewards

McDonald's $MCD is naming Uber $UBER the preferred delivery partner for orders placed in the McDonald's app as part of a multi-year partnership expansion across 14 markets, the companies announced on Monday.

The markets are the U.S., Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland and the U.K., the companies said. Uber Eats will serve as the preferred integrated delivery fulfillment partner for McDonald's app orders in participating markets, including the U.S., Australia, Canada, France, Germany and the U.K.

Uber Direct, Uber's white-label delivery service, will handle most of those orders in partnership with Deliverect, the companies said. Customers will be able to order delivery and track it from checkout to doorstep without leaving the McDonald's app. They can still order McDonald's through the Uber Eats app.

McDonald's and Uber first partnered in 2017 in the U.S. McDonald's is available on Uber Eats in 30 countries, the companies said.

Uber will be McDonald's exclusive delivery and rideshare rewards partner in participating markets. Starting this month, MyMcDonald's Rewards members in select markets can trade their points for Uber ride discounts via a seasonal activation in the McDonald's app. The companies plan to add features that would let customers earn MyMcDonald's Rewards points on eligible McDonald's orders placed through Uber Eats and redeem them for rewards, including Uber ride offers.

McDonald's has handed delivery orders to Uber or DoorDash interchangeably until now, according to Bloomberg. The new agreement puts Uber first in the markets it covers, and McDonald's will still appear as a restaurant choice on both companies' apps. McDonald's counts over 45 million U.S. loyalty members who use its app.

"McDelivery has grown into a global business of more than $20 billion a year," Mason Smoot, McDonald's senior vice president for global franchising and delivery, said in a statement.

"This marks our broadest expansion with McDonald's to date," Andrew Macdonald, Uber's president and chief operating officer, said in a statement.

DoorDash agreed last month to acquire Instacart in a deal with an equity value near $17 billion. The deal is expected to close at the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.

#5580. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to having extramarital affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia Corp. said on Sunday it’s launching an “independent investigation” into reports that its founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence plot, shortly after he admitted he “had been intimate” with a Singapore-based executive whom U.S. officials accuse of spying for China.

In response to the allegations, the Republican-led foreign affairs and intelligence committee of the U.S. Congress has asked Huang (pictured, right) to testify this week at a closed-door briefing on the chipmaker’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.” The request came after the New York Times reported last month that the CEO had been targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.

The accused spy is a woman called Alice Huang or Huang Le (left), of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. Alice Huang is the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed. It had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s high-end graphics processing units to China, prompting U.S. officials to begin monitoring her. Those officials have apparently determined that Alice Huang is an asset of the Chinese intelligence services, tasked with passing commercial secrets back to Beijing.

In a statement earlier today, Nvidia’s board of directors said that though it has no reason to believe that either U.S. national security or the company’s secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the statement said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The company added that Huang supports the investigation into what happened and has vowed to cooperate fully.

A report by Axios earlier today cited a draft email written by Huang to company employees, in which he admitted to having an illicit romantic relationship with Alice Huang and took full responsibility for his actions. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

U.S. intelligence chiefs will be concerned because Nvidia’s powerful chips sit at the center of the artificial intelligence boom and give America a critical advantage over its geopolitical rivals. The company’s dominance of AI computing means that Huang is one of the most influential people in the industry, and he has forged close ties with the Trump administration.

The alleged spy reportedly tried to take advantage of Huang’s close links to America’s policymakers. Not only was she tasked with learning more about the company’s secrets, but also persuading Huang to lobby for the company to be allowed to ship its most advanced processors to China.

It’s not clear how much influence she was able to exert on Huang, but last year he successfully petitioned the Trump administration to allow more GPUs to be exported to China. He later struck a deal to sell limited numbers of the company’s second-most powerful chips to China.

So far, nothing has been said of Huang potentially losing his job or being removed from the company, but Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives told Gizmodo that such an outcome is possible. “This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” the analyst said.

The investigation follows a rough week for technology firms on Wall Street, which have weathered a selloff that began earlier this month and gained traction after a series of disappointing earnings results in recent days. So far this month, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index has lost almost $1 trillion in value.

Nvidia’s stock has fallen 21% over the last month and is now basically flat in the year to date. Its market capitalization sits at just over $4.5 trillion, down from its peak of just over $5.7 trillion in October.

#5578. BMW is adding South Korean battery makers to cut its reliance on China

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Samsung SDI will supply cells in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the U.S. for BMW's sixth-generation batteries from the late 2020s

BMW has contracted South Korean battery makers Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution as additional cell suppliers for its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, the company said on Monday.

Samsung SDI will supply BMW from its established plants in Europe, and LG Energy Solution will do so from its established plants in the U.S. Deliveries start in the late 2020s, BMW said. In Europe, the company will now source cells from Chinese suppliers CATL and EVE Energy, as well as Samsung SDI.

BMW said it applies a "local for local" principle, buying components close to where vehicles are built. The company said this shortens transport distances and increases supply security, and that a globally diversified supplier network supports resilience and flexibility.

“Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” said Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW, in a statement.

BMW assembles its sixth-generation batteries at five new facilities built near its vehicle plants. They are in Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria, Debrecen in Hungary, Shenyang in China, Woodruff in the U.S. and San Luis Potosí in Mexico, according to the company.

BMW is ramping up worldwide output of the batteries, which run the carmaker's latest lineup of electric vehicles, including the iX3 SUV, according to Bloomberg.

The move fits a wider effort among automakers in Europe and the U.S. to become less dependent on parts from Chinese suppliers, according to Bloomberg. China leads the world in making batteries and in refining the key materials that go into them, Bloomberg said, a position that leaves automakers in Europe and North America vulnerable when it comes to capacity near their factories.

In September, analysts and executives said U.S. government funding falls short of what is needed to reduce China's hold on the global battery supply chain. China accounts for roughly four-fifths of all battery cells made worldwide, according to the International Energy Agency.

BMW also completed a $1.7 billion investment in its South Carolina operations in June, including the Woodruff plant. Woodruff is to supply high-voltage batteries for at least six fully electric models that BMW plans to assemble in the U.S. by 2030.

#5577. Mortgage rates fell and demand steadied as inventory dipped

Inventory declined week over week to 902,740 as mortgage rates eased for 3 straight weeks. With spreads at 2.27%, the path to sub-7% mortgage rates can happen with lower bond yields or better mortgage spreads.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates fell, demand stabilized and inventory had a noticeable decline last week. But are the changes in demand and inventory data about seasonality, or has the housing market changed with the recent mortgage rate decline? Let’s take a look at the weekend tracker and see what the data is telling us with rates falling the last three weeks.

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

What a crazy time in the bond market recently: the key level of 5.35% has not only held since early October, but the reversal has been truly nice to watch. The midterm elections, which changed the control of the House and Senate, have added another variable into the mortgage rate equation. I discussed what Congress can do to help lower mortgage rates on this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler, but for now the head-and-shoulders pattern of the 10-year yield is still somewhat intact, though a fight for it to break lower is happening.

I wouldn’t get too excited about mortgage rates until the 10-year yield can break under 4.70% and have follow-through bond buying, but mortgage rates have fallen and demand has stabilized over the last few weeks.

Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multiyear lows. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% —  spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility.That said, if mortgage spreads weren’t near multiyear lows right now, we’d have no chance of getting mortgage rates below 7.25%, and demand wouldn’t have stabilized recently. Now that spreads have moved up from this year’s lows, we can clearly see that mortgage rates would be sub-7% if spreads return to that level.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.27% from 2.23% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

The key for the last three weeks: lower rates, even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, this isn’t growth, just stabilization from a noticeable slowdown when mortgage rates got toward 7.60%. The last three years and 10 months show that housing demand grows when mortgage rates fall below 6.64% and head toward 6%; above 7%, we don’t have much growth data beyond seasonal demand. Last year at this time, mortgage rates were headed toward 6%, so the year-over-year comps will be hard for some time.

Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We had a small decline week to week; I can see the stabilization here as well and the year-over-year comps will also be very difficult here, as last year at this time rates were heading toward 6%. Earlier in the year, when rates were lower, pretty much every week this year showed growth.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks being down year over year. However, when mortgage rates got above 6.64% and then headed toward 7.60%, we did see some growth pick up. Also, rates were lower last year so demand was heading toward a nine-month high in December, which means it the comps will be easier to show growth in inventory.

Inventory growth is running at 7.18% even with easier comps.

New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 new listings per week a few times this year. The concern I had was that if higher rates cause sellers to stop listing their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 — that would hurt supply and demand. However, that hasn’t happened in any meaningful way. Most home sellers are buyers, and now that rates have fallen a smidge, it looks like we can end the year on a positive note for 2026 for new listings.

In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%; demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indexes show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown.

You want to keep an eye on how AI stocks trade this week, in particular CoreWeave’s stock price and how the 10-year yield reacts. For now, there’s an interesting correlation between the two, but I expect it to fade over time.

It’s inflation week again, with both CPI and PPI reports. Over the next 12 months, if the Iran conflict ends and the trade war doesn’t get worse, the question is whether bond traders will put more weight on those two factors than on the current inflation reports, which could improve in the future. This would be a huge positive for mortgage rates, but still, it will take a lot of work to end the trade war and the conflict. Existing home sales will come out and it won’t be pretty. We also have a lot of Fed speeches this week and it’s critical now to see what they say and how the bond market reacts to their talking points. Also, with the midterms over, I will be watching whether any of them start to talk about the end of the conflict and trade war being a positive for their future outlook.

#5576. CREFC Releases Updated Data Center Primer Amid Growth and Increasing Complexity in Financing Markets

Second edition examines expanding capital markets, regulatory developments, rising borrowing costs, and power constraints shaping data center investment

NEW YORK, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The CRE Finance Council (CREFC) today announced the release of the second edition of its Data Center Primer, providing an updated examination of the rapidly evolving financing market for data centers and the opportunities and risks facing commercial real estate lenders and investors.

Since CREFC published its inaugural primer in January 2026, the data center financing market has continued to expand and become increasingly complex. The updated report examines the growing use of securitization and secured project bonds, recent regulatory developments, higher borrowing costs, and the power and infrastructure constraints affecting development and financing decisions.

The scale of the market is substantial. As of October 8, 2026, Barclays counted approximately $116 billion of secured project bonds outstanding in the data center sector, alongside $44.2 billion in asset-backed securities (ABS) and $22.4 billion in commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS).

"Data centers have emerged as an increasingly important segment of the financing markets. This includes but is not limited to CMBS, ABS, Corporate Bonds and Syndicated Bank Loans. The sector is attracting significant equity and debt investors," said Paul T. Vanderslice, President and CEO of CREFC. "As the market evolves, CREFC is committed to providing the information and resources that help investors, lenders and other market participants better understand the opportunities and risks shaping this rapidly changing sector."

Key developments examined in the second edition include:

"While demand for data center capacity remains strong, lenders and investors need to look beyond traditional real estate fundamentals to fully assess the credit risks associated with these assets," said Raj Aidasani, Managing Director, Research at CREFC. "Power availability, infrastructure costs, tenant obligations, and refinancing assumptions can all have significant implications for a project's economics. Our updated primer examines how these factors intersect with evolving financing structures and what market participants should consider when evaluating transactions."

The second edition builds on CREFC's ongoing efforts to provide research, education, and market intelligence to support informed decision-making across the commercial real estate finance industry.

The CREFC Data Center Primer, Second Edition, is available here.

About CREFCThe CRE Finance Council (CREFC) is the trade association for the over $6 trillion commercial real estate finance industry with a membership that includes more than 400 companies and 19,000 individuals. Member firms include balance sheet and securitized lenders, loan and bond investors, private equity firms, servicers, rating agencies, and borrowers. For over 30 years, CREFC has promoted liquidity, transparency, and efficiency in the commercial real estate finance markets, and acted as a legislative and regulatory advocate for the industry, playing a vital role in setting market standards and best practices, and providing education for market participants. For more information, visit www.crefc.org.

#5575. Bitcoin ETF Attracts $75M as Goldman Sachs Calls December Fed Rate Cut

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin ETF demand returned on November 4 as Bitcoin recovered above $81,000, but Wall Street’s outlook for Federal Reserve rate cuts remains uncertain. Goldman Sachs pushed its expected Fed rate cuts back by one quarter, citing persistent inflation and a labor market that remains resilient. The bank now expects reductions in December 2026 and March 2027.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded $74.6 million in net inflows, ending three consecutive sessions of withdrawals totaling $1.16 billion. Fidelity’s FBTC led the recovery, while BlackRock’s IBIT continued losing capital.

Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund attracted approximately $236.7 million on November 4. Bitwise’s BITB added $15.2 million, while ARK Invest’s ARKB received $19.9 million.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust moved in the opposite direction, recording $201.2 million in outflows. The withdrawals extended IBIT’s four-session losing streak to $935 million. These mixed flows show that institutional demand has not returned uniformly across the market.

Bitcoin also recovered from a seven-week low near $75,600 during the November 3 election period, climbing back above $81,000 today. The rebound followed market stabilization after the U.S. midterm elections, although analysts cautioned against attributing the recovery to a single catalyst.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to deliver its next two rate cuts in December 2026 and March 2027, pushing both reductions back by one quarter.

The revised forecast shows concerns that energy costs could keep core personal consumption expenditures inflation near 3% throughout the year. Goldman economist David Mericle said lower inflation readings and further labor market softening would likely be necessary for the Fed to cut rates before year-end.

The bank maintained its projected terminal rate range of 3% to 3.25%, while acknowledging that the Fed could decide against additional cuts if economic conditions remain strong.

Bank of America adopted an even more cautious outlook, removing its expected 2026 rate cuts and moving them into the third quarter of 2027. This shift creates a more challenging macro backdrop for Bitcoin, which often benefits when borrowing costs fall and liquidity conditions improve.

But the latest Bitcoin ETF inflows suggest some investors are still willing to increase exposure despite the delayed easing outlook. The contrast between returning fund demand and a more cautious Fed forecast gives Bitcoin traders two competing signals.

Institutional buying could help support prices if inflows continue, while elevated interest rates may limit the liquidity available for risk assets.
